q.st: A nursing student is reviewing the pathophysiology of childhood leukemia. Which cellular mechanism accounts for the anemia, infection, and bleeding seen at diagnosis?
o: A
Proliferating immature blast cells crowd and depress normal bone marrow hematopoiesis
Immature leukocytes depress bone marrow production of erythrocytes, neutrophils, and platelets.
B
Excessive splenic destruction of mature lymphocytes triggers autoimmune hemolysis
Bone marrow depression by immature blast cells causes pancytopenia rather than isolated splenic hemolysis.
C
Elevated erythropoietin levels inhibit platelet maturation in peripheral blood vessels
Decreased erythrocyte production causes anemia rather than elevated erythropoietin levels inhibiting platelets.
D
Hyperactive megakaryocytes consume circulating clotting factors and white blood cells
Platelet production is decreased in leukemia, causing thrombocytopenia rather than megakaryocyte hyperactivity.
q.obj: Proliferating immature blast cells depress the bone marrow, causing anemia, neutropenia-related infection, and thrombocytopenia.
fc: Malignant increase in immature leukocytes (blast cells) in bone marrow | Depresses marrow: anemia (low RBCs), infection (neutropenia), bleeding (thrombocytopenia) | Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) is most frequent childhood cancer

q.st: The nurse is conducting an educational session on pediatric oncology epidemiology. Which malignancy is the most frequent type of cancer occurring in children?
o: A
Acute lymphocytic leukemia
Acute lymphocytic leukemia is the most common malignant neoplasm diagnosed in pediatric clients.
B
Osteogenic sarcoma
Osteosarcoma is the most common childhood bone cancer but occurs less frequently than leukemia.
C
Nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumor)
Wilms' tumor is the most common pediatric kidney tumor rather than the overall most frequent cancer.
D
Hodgkin's lymphoma
Hodgkin's disease peaks in midadolescence and is less common overall than acute lymphocytic leukemia.
q.obj: Acute lymphocytic leukemia is the most frequent type of cancer in children.
fc: Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL): most frequent cancer in children | Wilms' tumor: most common intra-abdominal/kidney tumor (peak age 3) | Osteosarcoma: most common pediatric bone cancer (peak age 13-16)

q.st: The parent of a 5-year-old child newly diagnosed with acute lymphocytic leukemia asks why the chemotherapy protocol includes intrathecal medication during central nervous system prophylactic therapy. What is the nurse's best explanation?
o: A
It prevents leukemic blast cells from invading the central nervous system
Central nervous system prophylactic therapy specifically prevents leukemic cells from invading the CNS.
B
It achieves initial complete remission by eliminating systemic bone marrow blasts
Induction therapy achieves initial complete remission, whereas CNS prophylaxis prevents central nervous invasion.
C
It reduces residual systemic tumor burden immediately following initial induction
Intensification or consolidation therapy further decreases systemic tumor burden after induction remission.
D
It serves as long-term low-dose therapy over several years to sustain remission
Maintenance therapy preserves long-term remission after induction, consolidation, and CNS prophylaxis.
q.obj: Leukemia chemotherapy phases include induction (remission), intensification/consolidation (reduce tumor burden), CNS prophylaxis (prevent CNS invasion), and maintenance.
fc: 1. Induction: achieves complete remission | 2. Intensification/consolidation: decreases tumor burden further | 3. CNS prophylaxis: prevents CNS invasion | 4. Maintenance: sustains remission

q.st: A 4-year-old child is admitted with pallor, fatigue, easy bruising, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Which diagnostic test result confirms the suspected diagnosis of acute lymphocytic leukemia?
o: A
Bone marrow biopsy specimen demonstrating leukemic blast-phase cells
A positive bone marrow biopsy identifying immature blast-phase cells confirms the diagnosis of leukemia.
B
Lumbar puncture showing clear cerebrospinal fluid without blast cells
A lumbar puncture evaluates central nervous system involvement rather than confirming primary leukemia.
C
Complete blood count showing a white blood cell count of 4,500 mm3
White blood cell counts may be normal, high, or low in leukemia and are not diagnostic.
D
Peripheral blood smear showing a platelet count of 350,000 mm3
Platelet counts are typically decreased in leukemia and cannot independently establish a definitive diagnosis.
q.obj: A positive bone marrow biopsy identifying leukemic blast cells confirms leukemia; a lumbar puncture assesses for CNS involvement.
fc: Confirmatory test: bone marrow biopsy positive for leukemic blast cells | Lumbar puncture: detects blast cells in CSF (CNS involvement) | CBC: low Hgb/Hct, low platelets, normal/high/low WBC

q.st: The nurse is assessing a 6-year-old child admitted with newly diagnosed acute lymphocytic leukemia. Which clinical manifestations are consistent with malignant bone marrow infiltration? Select all that apply.
o: A
Fever, pallor, and persistent fatigue
Anemia and neutropenia from marrow replacement produce characteristic pallor, fatigue, and fever.
B
Petechiae and easy bruising on the extremities
Thrombocytopenia from marrow depression leads to mucocutaneous hemorrhage such as petechiae and bruising.
C
Bone and joint pain with risk for pathological fractures
Infiltration of leukemic cells into bone marrow causes bone pain and weakens skeletal integrity.
D
Hypertension caused by excessive renin secretion
Renin-mediated hypertension is characteristic of Wilms' tumor rather than leukemic marrow infiltration.
E
Musty urine odor and hypopigmentation of the hair
Musty urine odor and hypopigmentation occur in untreated phenylketonuria rather than childhood leukemia.
q.obj: Bone marrow infiltration in leukemia causes fever, pallor, fatigue, anorexia, hemorrhage (petechiae), bone/joint pain, and pathological fractures.
fc: Marrow infiltration: fever, pallor, fatigue, anorexia, petechiae, bone/joint pain | Organ invasion: hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, CNS, kidneys, testes | Cranial nerve VII (facial) most commonly affected

q.st: A child with central nervous system involvement from acute lymphocytic leukemia is evaluated for cranial nerve deficits. Which cranial nerve is most commonly affected in childhood leukemia?
o: A
Cranial nerve VII (facial nerve)
Cranial nerve VII, the facial nerve, is the most frequently affected cranial nerve in leukemia.
B
Cranial nerve I (olfactory nerve)
The olfactory nerve is rarely involved compared with the facial nerve in CNS leukemia.
C
Cranial nerve XI (spinal accessory nerve)
Spinal accessory nerve palsy is uncommon relative to cranial nerve VII involvement in leukemia.
D
Cranial nerve XII (hypoglossal nerve)
Hypoglossal nerve dysfunction occurs far less frequently than facial nerve involvement in CNS leukemia.
q.obj: In childhood leukemia with central nervous system involvement, cranial nerve VII (the facial nerve) is most commonly affected.
fc: Lumbar puncture checks spinal fluid for leukemic blast cells | Most commonly affected cranial nerve: CN VII (facial nerve) | Monitor closely for signs of increased ICP (Box 32.1)

q.st: The nurse is assessing a 5-month-old infant with central nervous system leukemia for increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Which infant-specific signs indicate increased ICP? Select all that apply.
o: A
Tense, bulging anterior fontanel and separated cranial sutures
Open cranial sutures in infants expand under rising intracranial pressure, causing a bulging fontanel.
B
Macewen's sign (cracked-pot sound on skull percussion) and high-pitched cry
Skull percussion resonance and a shrill high-pitched cry are classic infant cues of increased ICP.
C
Setting sun sign with sclera visible above the downward-deviated iris
Downward eye deviation exposing upper sclera is a hallmark neurological sign of infant ICP.
D
Complaints of severe frontal headache and diplopia
Infants cannot verbalize subjective complaints of frontal headache or double vision.
E
Decline in school performance and inability to follow written commands
School performance decline applies to older children rather than a 5-month-old infant.
q.obj: Infant signs of increased ICP include tense bulging fontanel, separated sutures, Macewen's sign, high-pitched cry, increased head circumference, distended scalp veins, and setting sun sign.
fc: Tense bulging fontanel, separated sutures, increased head circumference | Macewen's sign (cracked-pot sound), distended scalp veins | High-pitched cry, irritability, poor feeding, setting sun sign

q.st: The nurse is monitoring a 3-year-old child following a craniotomy for early signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Which clinical finding should the nurse monitor for as an early indicator in this toddler?
o: A
Vomiting
Because fontanels are closed by age 3, vomiting from medullary pressure is an early sign.
B
Bulging anterior fontanel
The anterior fontanel closes between 12 and 18 months and no longer bulges at age 3.
C
Increasing head circumference
Cranial sutures fuse after infancy, preventing head circumference enlargement in a 3-year-old child.
D
Decerebrate posturing with bradycardia
Decerebrate posturing and bradycardia represent late, life-threatening signs of brainstem compression.
q.obj: Once fontanels close (posterior at 2-3 months; anterior at 12-18 months), early signs of increased ICP include vomiting, nausea, headache, diplopia, and seizures.
fc: Childhood Early Increased ICP Signs (Box 32.1 & PQ 6)

Fontanel closure: posterior 2-3 mo, anterior 12-18 mo | Child early ICP signs: headache, nausea, forceful vomiting, diplopia, seizures | Behavioral signs: irritability, drowsiness, school decline, lethargy

q.st: A 9-year-old child with central nervous system leukemia becomes acutely unresponsive in the pediatric intensive care unit. Which assessment findings indicate late, life-threatening increased intracranial pressure? Select all that apply.
o: A
Bradycardia and Cheyne-Stokes respirations
Brainstem compression produces slowing heart rate and periodic Cheyne-Stokes respiratory patterns in late ICP.
B
Decerebrate (extension) or decorticate (flexion) posturing
Abnormal motor posturing indicates severe descending cerebral and brainstem herniation.
C
Alterations in pupil size and reaction with papilledema
Cranial nerve III compression and optic disc swelling reflect dangerously elevated intracranial pressure.
D
Restlessness with mild irritability and decreased school focus
Restlessness and declining school performance are early behavioral cues rather than late decompensation.
E
Nausea with occasional morning diplopia
Nausea and diplopia represent early childhood manifestations rather than late brainstem herniation.
q.obj: Late signs of increased ICP include bradycardia, Cheyne-Stokes respirations, pupil alterations, papilledema, decorticate/decerebrate posturing, decreased consciousness, and coma.
fc: Bradycardia and Cheyne-Stokes respirations | Pupil size/reaction changes and papilledema | Decorticate or decerebrate posturing, decreased consciousness, coma

q.st: A 7-year-old child receiving induction chemotherapy for acute lymphocytic leukemia develops a temperature of 38.4 C (101.1 F) while severely neutropenic. Which sequence of actions should the nurse implement?
o: A
Obtain blood cultures and a CBC with differential, then initiate prescribed antibiotics
Cultures and a CBC with differential must be drawn before starting broad-spectrum antibiotics.
B
Administer oral acetaminophen and recheck the temperature in 4 hours before notifying the provider
Neutropenic fever is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate cultures and antibiotic therapy.
C
Obtain a rectal temperature to confirm core fever before drawing laboratory specimens
Rectal thermometers are strictly contraindicated in neutropenic children due to mucosal trauma and sepsis.
D
Administer prescribed granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and withhold antibiotics until cultures finalize
Antibiotics are initiated immediately after cultures are obtained rather than delayed for final results.
q.obj: If a child with cancer develops a fever while neutropenic, cultures and a CBC with differential are drawn first, then antibiotics are started.
fc: Common infection sites: skin, respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract | Neutropenic fever action: draw cultures + CBC with differential FIRST | Start prescribed antibiotics immediately afterward

q.st: The nurse is implementing protective isolation precautions for a hospitalized child with severe chemotherapy-induced neutropenia. Which interventions help protect the child from infection? Select all that apply.
o: A
Maintain the child in a private room with HEPA filtration and strict handwashing
Private rooms with HEPA filtration and thorough handwashing minimize airborne and contact pathogen transmission.
B
Eliminate raw fruits, raw vegetables, fresh flowers, and standing water from the room
Raw produce, soil, and standing water harbor molds and bacteria such as Aspergillus and Pseudomonas.
C
Ensure anyone entering the room wears a mask and use strict aseptic technique
Masking entrants and maintaining strict asepsis protect the immunosuppressed child from cross-contamination.
D
Place the child in a semiprivate room with another afebrile pediatric client
Sharing a room exposes the neutropenic child to contagious pathogens from roommates and visitors.
E
Measure core body temperature rectally every 4 hours for accuracy
Rectal temperatures risk mucosal tears and life-threatening bacteremia in neutropenic pediatric clients.
q.obj: Protective isolation includes a private HEPA-filtered room, handwashing, masks, strict asepsis, no raw fruits/vegetables/flowers/standing water, and avoiding invasive procedures.
fc: Private room with HEPA/laminar airflow; masks for entrants; strict asepsis | No raw fruits/vegetables, fresh flowers, or standing water | Daily antimicrobial bath, oral hygiene, avoid rectal/invasive procedures

q.st: The grandparent of a 6-year-old neutropenic child in protective isolation brings a fresh bouquet of garden flowers and asks the nurse for a vase. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: A
Your flowers are lovely, but fresh flowers cannot be kept in the room due to infection risk
Standing water and damp soil harbor Aspergillus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, posing lethal infection risks.
B
I will wash a vase with antimicrobial soap so the flowers can stay by the window
Washing the vase does not eliminate fungal spores and bacteria present on fresh flowers.
C
You may place the flowers on the far bedside stand at least 6 feet from the bed
Fresh flowers and standing water are completely prohibited anywhere inside a neutropenic client's room.
D
Only potted plants with dry soil are permitted in protective isolation rooms
Both potted plants and cut flowers harbor molds and bacteria and must be excluded.
q.obj: Fresh flowers, plants, and standing water must not be kept in a neutropenic child's room because they harbor Aspergillus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
fc: No fresh flowers or potted plants (harbor Aspergillus & Pseudomonas) | No standing water in the child's room | Eliminate raw fruits and vegetables from diet (harbor molds)

q.st: The parents of a 4-year-old child receiving chemotherapy for acute lymphocytic leukemia ask which routine childhood immunizations are safe to administer during immunosuppression. Which vaccine may be safely administered?
o: A
Salk inactivated poliomyelitis vaccine
The inactivated Salk polio vaccine contains killed virus and may be safely given during immunosuppression.
B
Measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine
Live attenuated MMR virus can cause life-threatening systemic infection in an immunosuppressed child.
C
Varicella live attenuated vaccine
Varicella is a live virus vaccine and is strictly contraindicated while the immune system is depressed.
D
Oral live attenuated poliovirus vaccine
Live oral polio vaccine risks vaccine-associated paralytic infection in an immunocompromised child.
q.obj: Immunosuppressed children must not receive live virus vaccines (MMR, live polio, varicella), whereas the Salk inactivated polio vaccine may be administered.
fc: CONTRAINDICATED live vaccines: MMR, live polio, varicella (risk life-threatening infection) | SAFE: Salk (inactivated) vaccine for poliomyelitis | Notify school teacher to report communicable diseases immediately

q.st: The nurse reviews morning laboratory results for a child receiving chemotherapy and notes a platelet count of 19,500 mm3 (19.5 x 10^9/L). Which priority intervention should the nurse incorporate into the plan of care?
o: A
Initiate bleeding precautions
A platelet count below 50,000 mm3 places the child at high risk for spontaneous hemorrhage.
B
Initiate airborne protective isolation precautions
Airborne protective isolation addresses severe neutropenia rather than isolated low platelet counts.
C
Administer ibuprofen every 6 hours for bone discomfort
NSAIDs and aspirin impair platelet aggregation and are strictly avoided in thrombocytopenic children.
D
Encourage vigorous daily flossing to prevent gingival hyperplasia
Dental floss causes gingival trauma and bleeding and must be avoided during thrombocytopenia.
q.obj: A platelet count below 50,000 mm3 (50.0 x 10^9/L) requires immediate bleeding precautions to prevent hemorrhage.
fc: Platelet count < 50,000 mm3 -> initiate bleeding precautions | Platelet transfusions generally reserved for active bleeding unresponsive to local care | Packed RBCs prescribed for severe blood loss

q.st: The nurse is caring for a 9-year-old child with severe chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia. Which interventions should be included in the bleeding precautions plan? Select all that apply.
o: A
Use a soft toothbrush, avoid dental floss, and serve cool-to-warm soft foods
Gentle oral care and non-irritating soft foods prevent mucosal trauma and gingival hemorrhage.
B
Apply firm, gentle pressure to any needlestick site for at least 10 minutes
Prolonged direct pressure for at least 10 minutes ensures stable clot formation after venipuncture.
C
Measure abdominal girth daily and examine all body fluids and excrement for blood
Increasing abdominal girth signals occult internal hemorrhage, while inspecting excretions detects early bleeding.
D
Administer rectal acetaminophen suppositories if mild fever develops
Rectal suppositories, enemas, and thermometers risk mucosal injury and severe hemorrhage.
E
Encourage the child to blow the nose forcefully to clear nasal crusts
Forceful nose blowing disrupts fragile nasal capillaries and precipitates severe epistaxis.
q.obj: Bleeding precautions include soft toothbrush, no floss, cool/warm soft foods, 10-minute needlestick pressure, padded rails, no NSAIDs/aspirin, no nose blowing, and no rectal procedures.
fc: Soft toothbrush, no floss, cool-to-warm soft foods; no nose blowing | Avoid injections; hold firm pressure on needlesticks >= 10 minutes | Measure abdominal girth; check all excrement for blood; avoid NSAIDs/aspirin/rectal items

q.st: The nurse is providing home discharge teaching to the parents of a 10-year-old child with leukemia who has a platelet count of 32,000 mm3 (32 x 10^9/L). Which instruction regarding over-the-counter medications is essential?
o: A
Avoid administering nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and products containing aspirin
NSAIDs and aspirin inhibit platelet function and dramatically increase the risk of severe hemorrhage.
B
Give low-dose chewable aspirin for mild bone aches to prevent clot formation
Aspirin is strictly contraindicated in thrombocytopenic children due to irreversible platelet inhibition.
C
Administer ibuprofen before bedtime to prevent nocturnal joint stiffness
Ibuprofen is an NSAID that impairs hemostasis and must be avoided during thrombocytopenia.
D
Use bismuth subsalicylate liquid if mild nausea or loose stools occur
Bismuth subsalicylate contains salicylate (aspirin-related compound) and must be avoided in bleeding risk.
q.obj: Parents of a thrombocytopenic child must avoid administering NSAIDs and any products containing aspirin.
fc: Avoid NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) and all aspirin-containing products | Count pads/tampons if adolescent is menstruating | Pad sharp furniture corners and avoid tight/constrictive clothing

q.st: A child with acute lymphocytic leukemia has a platelet count of 28,000 mm3 (28 x 10^9/L) and no active bleeding. The parent asks why the health care provider has not ordered a prophylactic platelet transfusion today. What is the nurse's best explanation?
o: A
Platelet transfusions are generally reserved for active bleeding episodes unresponsive to local treatment
Platelet transfusions are typically reserved for active bleeding not controlled by local measures.
B
Platelet transfusions are contraindicated during induction and relapse chemotherapy phases
Platelet transfusions are specifically utilized when active bleeding occurs during induction or relapse therapy.
C
Packed red blood cells are always transfused first to stimulate endogenous platelet release
Packed red blood cells treat severe blood loss anemia rather than stimulating platelet production.
D
Platelet transfusions cannot be administered until the white blood cell count exceeds 10,000 mm3
Platelet transfusion decisions depend on active bleeding status rather than white blood cell thresholds.
q.obj: Platelet transfusions are generally reserved for active bleeding episodes that do not respond to local treatment and may occur during induction or relapse.
fc: Platelet transfusions: reserved for active bleeding unresponsive to local measures (induction/relapse) | Packed RBCs: prescribed for severe blood loss | Monitor closely for transfusion reactions

q.st: A 6-year-old child receiving chemotherapy for leukemia experiences severe fatigue and oral mucositis. Which nursing interventions best promote energy conservation and adequate nutrition? Select all that apply.
o: A
Provide small meals that require minimal chewing and do not irritate oral mucosa
Small, soft, non-irritating meals reduce energy expenditure and prevent pain from oral mucositis.
B
Cluster essential care activities and allow frequent, uninterrupted rest periods
Eliminating nonessential tasks and spacing care preserves limited energy reserves during marrow suppression.
C
Administer frequent prescribed mouth rinses and local oral anesthetics as ordered
Soothing mouth rinses and topical anesthetics promote mucosal healing, prevent infection, and ease eating.
D
Serve three large, high-fiber raw vegetable meals daily to boost caloric intake
Large meals exhaust the fatigued child, and raw vegetables pose a bacterial/fungal infection hazard.
E
Wake the child every 2 hours throughout the night to perform routine hygiene
Interrupting sleep for nonessential care worsens exhaustion and impairs recovery.
q.obj: For fatigue and mucositis, provide small non-irritating meals, frequent mouth rinses, clustered essential care with rest periods, and enteral/parenteral nutrition if needed.
fc: Small meals requiring little chewing; non-irritating to mucosa | Allow adequate rest periods; perform only essential nursing care | Frequent mouth rinses and prescribed local oral anesthetics for mucositis

q.st: The nurse is monitoring a child 10 days after receiving high-dose combination chemotherapy and notes that blood cell counts have dropped to their lowest point (the nadir). Which complication poses the greatest immediate threat to the child's life?
o: A
Overwhelming infection without typical inflammatory signs due to severe immunosuppression
Infection is a major cause of death, and immunosuppressed children may lack classic symptoms.
B
Permanent alopecia that fails to regrow after chemotherapy completion
Chemotherapy-induced alopecia is temporary, with hair regrowing within 3 to 6 months.
C
Acute hypertension caused by excessive red blood cell overproduction
Bone marrow suppression at the nadir causes anemia and hypotension rather than polycythemia.
D
Rapid weight gain caused by increased gastrointestinal motility
Chemotherapy typically causes nausea, vomiting, and anorexia rather than rapid weight gain.
q.obj: Children receiving chemotherapy may not show typical signs of infection due to immunosuppression; infection is a major cause of death.
fc: Nadir: period of greatest bone marrow suppression (blood counts lowest) | Immunosuppressed children may NOT present with typical signs of infection | Infection is a major cause of death -> monitor closely

q.st: The nurse is caring for a child receiving intravenous cyclophosphamide and vincristine chemotherapy. Which adverse effects should the nurse specifically monitor for during treatment? Select all that apply.
o: A
Hemorrhagic cystitis
Chemotherapeutic agents can irritate the bladder mucosa, requiring close monitoring for hematuria and dysuria.
B
Peripheral neuropathy
Neurotoxic chemotherapy requires monitoring for paresthesias, foot drop, constipation, and diminished reflexes.
C
Dehydration and constipation
Chemotherapy-induced vomiting, poor intake, and slowed bowel motility require hydration and stool softeners.
D
Permanent irreversible blindness
Ocular blindness is not a standard routine monitoring parameter listed for childhood leukemia chemotherapy.
E
Excessive bone overgrowth of the cranial vault
Chemotherapy suppresses rapidly dividing cells rather than causing cranial bone hypertrophy.
q.obj: During chemotherapy, monitor for nadir myelosuppression, infection, bleeding, dehydration, hemorrhagic cystitis, peripheral neuropathy, mucositis, and constipation.
fc: Monitor for hemorrhagic cystitis and peripheral neuropathy | Administer antiemetics before, during, and after chemotherapy | Administer stool softeners to prevent straining; gentle rectal hygiene

q.st: An 11-year-old girl scheduled to begin chemotherapy for acute lymphocytic leukemia cries and asks the nurse if her hair will ever grow back once it falls out. What is the nurse's most accurate response?
o: A
Your hair will regrow in about 3 to 6 months, though it may be a slightly different color or texture
Hair loss from chemotherapy is temporary and regrows in 3 to 6 months, often altered.
B
Your hair will grow back completely within 2 weeks of your very first chemotherapy dose
Hair regrowth requires completion of intensive marrow-suppressive cycles and takes 3 to 6 months.
C
Chemotherapy causes permanent hair loss, so we will help you select a permanent wig
Chemotherapy-induced alopecia in children is temporary and regrows within 3 to 6 months.
D
Your hair will only fall out if cranial radiation is given alongside oral medications
Systemic chemotherapy agents commonly cause temporary alopecia even without cranial radiation.
q.obj: Parents and children should be informed that hair loss from chemotherapy is temporary and regrows in about 3 to 6 months, possibly with a slightly different color or texture.
fc: Inform parents and child that hair loss may occur | Hair regrows in about 3 to 6 months | Regrown hair may have a slightly different color or texture

q.st: The parents of a 5-year-old child newly diagnosed with leukemia express overwhelming fear and isolation as treatment begins. Which psychosocial interventions should the nurse implement?
o: A
Encourage them to verbalize feelings, introduce them to other families, and consult social services
Active listening, peer family support, and social services or chaplaincy help families cope with diagnosis.
B
Discourage discussion of fears in front of the child to maintain a cheerful environment
Suppressing emotional expression increases family anxiety and prevents therapeutic psychosocial support.
C
Isolate the family from other oncology parents to prevent emotional distress
Connecting with other families of children with cancer provides valuable peer validation and support.
D
Delay social work referrals until the child enters the maintenance phase of therapy
Early social services and chaplain consultations provide essential emotional and financial resources from diagnosis.
q.obj: Psychosocial support for families of children with cancer includes active listening, peer family introductions, and social services/chaplain consultations.
fc: Listen and encourage child and family to verbalize feelings/concerns | Introduce family to other families of children with cancer | Consult social services and chaplains as necessary

q.st: A 15-year-old adolescent is undergoing diagnostic evaluation for suspected Hodgkin's disease after presenting with painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Which diagnostic test result confirms Hodgkin's disease?
o: A
Lymph node biopsy specimen demonstrating giant, multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells
The presence of characteristic Reed-Sternberg cells on lymph node biopsy confirms Hodgkin's disease.
B
Elevated 24-hour urine vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid levels
Elevated urinary catecholamine metabolites (VMA and HVA) indicate neuroblastoma rather than Hodgkin's disease.
C
Bone marrow aspirate containing greater than 25% immature lymphoblasts
Immature lymphoblasts in bone marrow confirm acute lymphocytic leukemia rather than Hodgkin's lymphoma.
D
Positive heterophile antibody test confirming acute Epstein-Barr mononucleosis
Epstein-Barr virus is associated with mononucleosis and does not confirm malignant Hodgkin's disease.
q.obj: Hodgkin's disease is a malignancy of the lymph nodes characterized by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells in a lymph node biopsy specimen.
fc: Malignancy of lymph nodes; peak incidence in midadolescence | Confirmatory finding: Reed-Sternberg cells on lymph node biopsy | Spreads predictably to spleen, liver, bone marrow, lungs, mediastinum

q.st: The nurse is reviewing the admission physical examination of a 14-year-old adolescent with advanced Hodgkin's disease. Which clinical cues are characteristic of this condition? Select all that apply.
o: A
Painless, firm, movable lymph nodes in the cervical and supraclavicular areas
Enlarged, firm, nontender, movable nodes—often starting at the left supraclavicular sentinel node—are classic.
B
Intermittent low-grade fevers, night sweats, weight loss, and pruritus
Advanced nodal and extralymphatic involvement produces systemic B-symptoms including fever, night sweats, and pruritus.
C
Nonproductive cough from mediastinal adenopathy and abdominal pain from retroperitoneal nodes
Enlarged mediastinal and retroperitoneal nodes compress adjacent airways and abdominal structures.
D
Painful, warm, fluctuant axillary nodes that drain purulent material
Tender, purulent lymph nodes indicate acute bacterial lymphadenitis rather than painless Hodgkin's nodes.
E
Supraorbital ecchymosis and exophthalmos from retrobulbar mass invasion
Periorbital ecchymosis and exophthalmos are classic metastatic signs of neuroblastoma rather than Hodgkin's.
q.obj: Hodgkin's disease cues include painless firm movable cervical/left supraclavicular ('sentinel') nodes, nonproductive cough, abdominal pain, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and pruritus.
fc: Painless, firm, movable cervical/left supraclavicular ('sentinel') nodes | Nonproductive cough (mediastinal), abdominal pain (retroperitoneal) | Systemic: low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, pruritus
Ch. 32 Section II.B & Clinical Judgment Box

q.st: A 16-year-old adolescent receiving extensive radiation therapy for Hodgkin's disease reports profound exhaustion and lack of motivation to attend school or see friends. Which radiation adverse effect does the nurse recognize as the most common cause?
o: A
Malaise, which is physically and psychologically difficult for adolescents to tolerate
Malaise is the most common adverse effect of extensive irradiation and strongly impacts adolescents.
B
Acute hemorrhagic cystitis caused by bladder mucosal ulceration
Bladder cystitis causes hematuria and dysuria rather than systemic exhaustion and social withdrawal.
C
Dry desquamation of the irradiated supraclavicular skin field
Local skin desquamation causes cutaneous dryness rather than systemic adolescent fatigue and malaise.
D
Cranial nerve VII palsy resulting from cerebellar radiation edema
Facial nerve palsy is associated with CNS leukemia or brainstem tumors rather than Hodgkin's radiation.
q.obj: The most common adverse effect of extensive irradiation is malaise, which can be difficult for older children and adolescents to tolerate physically and psychologically.
fc: Treatment: chemotherapy alone or combined with radiation therapy | Most common adverse effect of extensive irradiation: malaise | Malaise is physically and psychologically difficult for older children/adolescents

q.st: The nurse is caring for a child receiving external beam radiation therapy who develops dry desquamation and erythema over the irradiated chest skin. Which skin care interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
o: A
Keep the skin clean and wash daily using a mild soap sparingly
Gentle cleansing with mild soap preserves fragile irradiated epidermis without causing chemical irritation.
B
Leave all radiation skin markings intact and avoid sun or extreme temperature exposure
Radiation markings guide precise beam alignment, while sun and temperature extremes damage sensitized skin.
C
Apply prescribed topical lubricants for skin dryness
Prescribed lubricants soothe dry desquamation without interfering with radiation beam delivery.
D
Wash off the purple radiation ink markings daily with alcohol swabs
Removing radiation markings disrupts treatment targeting, and alcohol severely dries irradiated skin.
E
Apply a heating pad directly over the irradiated skin to relieve tightness
Extreme heat exposure causes severe thermal injury to radiation-sensitized skin.
q.obj: For radiation skin desquamation, wash daily with mild soap sparingly, do not remove radiation markings, avoid sun/temperature extremes, and apply prescribed lubricants.
fc: Skin: wash daily with mild soap sparingly; DO NOT remove radiation markings | Avoid sun exposure and extreme temperatures; apply prescribed lubricant | Alopecia: introduce wig/head wraps; stress head covering in cold weather

q.st: A school-age child undergoing pelvic and abdominal radiation therapy develops anorexia, mucosal ulcerations, and frequent diarrhea. Which nursing interventions align with radiation gastrointestinal care?
o: A
Provide small frequent meals, soothing oral rinses, prescribed antidiarrheals, and monitor hydration
Small meals, soothing oral hygiene, antidiarrheals, and dehydration monitoring manage GI radiation effects.
B
Restrict oral fluid intake to 500 mL daily to slow gastrointestinal peristalsis
Diarrhea and vomiting cause dehydration, requiring adequate fluid intake rather than fluid restriction.
C
Administer rectal antispasmodic suppositories before each radiation session
Rectal suppositories and enemas are contraindicated during radiation-induced bone marrow myelosuppression.
D
Brush oral mucosal ulcers vigorously with lemon-glycerin swabs after meals
Lemon-glycerin swabs irritate ulcerated mucosa; soothing oral hygiene and prescribed rinses are indicated.
q.obj: For radiation GI adverse effects, provide small frequent meals, around-the-clock antiemetics, soothing mouth rinses, prescribed antidiarrheals, and dehydration monitoring.
fc: GI: small frequent meals, around-the-clock antiemetics, soothing mouth rinses, antidiarrheals | Monitor closely for weight loss and dehydration | Bladder cystitis: encourage fluid intake, frequent voiding, monitor hematuria

q.st: A child receiving pelvic irradiation is at risk for radiation-induced urinary bladder cystitis. Which nursing interventions best prevent and detect this complication?
o: A
Encourage generous fluid intake, promote frequent voiding, and monitor urine for hematuria
High fluid intake and frequent voiding dilute bladder irritants, while hematuria monitoring detects cystitis.
B
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to keep the bladder continuously empty
Indwelling catheterization increases infection risk during myelosuppression and is unnecessary for routine cystitis prevention.
C
Limit fluids after 4 PM so the child holds urine overnight during sleep
Holding concentrated urine in the bladder prolongs mucosal irritation and worsens radiation cystitis.
D
Administer daily aspirin to prevent bladder microvascular thrombosis
Aspirin increases bleeding risk during radiation-induced myelosuppression and worsens hematuria.
q.obj: To manage radiation-induced urinary bladder cystitis, the nurse encourages fluid intake, promotes frequent voiding, and monitors for hematuria.
fc: Encourage generous oral/IV fluid intake | Promote frequent voiding to minimize mucosal contact | Monitor urine closely for hematuria

q.st: A child receiving extensive irradiation develops radiation-induced bone marrow myelosuppression. Which intervention is mandatory in the nursing plan of care?
o: A
Avoid suppositories, enemas, and rectal temperatures while instituting neutropenic/bleeding precautions
Rectal trauma can cause fatal hemorrhage or sepsis during radiation-induced bone marrow myelosuppression.
B
Encourage outdoor sunbathing to stimulate vitamin D-mediated marrow recovery
Sun exposure causes severe cutaneous burns on irradiated skin and must be strictly avoided.
C
Discontinue temperature monitoring unless the child reports chills
Fever monitoring is essential to detect early infection during radiation-induced myelosuppression.
D
Administer rectal acetaminophen if low-grade evening fever develops
Suppositories are strictly contraindicated in myelosuppressed clients due to bleeding and infection risk.
q.obj: For radiation-induced bone marrow myelosuppression, monitor for fever and anemia, administer prescribed antibiotics, institute neutropenic/bleeding precautions, and avoid rectal procedures.
fc: Monitor for fever and signs of anemia; give prescribed antibiotics | Avoid suppositories, enemas, and rectal temperatures | Institute neutropenic and bleeding precautions as needed

q.st: A 3-year-old child is admitted with a firm, nontender, unilateral flank mass suspected to be nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumor). Which epidemiological and clinical description accurately characterizes Wilms' tumor?
o: A
It is the most common intra-abdominal and kidney tumor of childhood, peaking at age 3
Wilms' tumor is the most common childhood kidney tumor, peaking at 3 years old.
B
It is a malignant bone tumor of the distal femur peaking between ages 13 and 16
Malignant distal femur tumors peaking in adolescence describe osteosarcoma rather than renal Wilms' tumor.
C
It originates from embryonic neural crest cells and typically crosses the abdominal midline
Neural crest tumors crossing the midline describe neuroblastoma rather than unilateral encapsulated Wilms' tumor.
D
It is a lymph node malignancy confirmed by multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells
Reed-Sternberg cells in lymph nodes characterize Hodgkin's disease rather than nephroblastoma.
q.obj: Wilms' tumor is the most common intra-abdominal and kidney tumor of childhood (peak age 3), associated with genetic inheritance and congenital anomalies.
fc: Most common intra-abdominal and kidney tumor of childhood | Peak incidence: 3 years of age; unilateral or bilateral | Associated with genetic inheritance and congenital anomalies

q.st: The nurse is assessing a 3-year-old child admitted with suspected Wilms' tumor. Which clinical manifestations should the nurse expect to observe? Select all that apply.
o: A
Firm, nontender abdominal flank mass confined to one side
Wilms' tumor typically presents as a firm, nontender, unilateral mass deep within the flank.
B
Hypertension caused by tumor secretion of excess renin
Renal compression and excess renin secretion by the tumor frequently produce systemic hypertension.
C
Hematuria, urinary retention, and pallor from intratumoral hemorrhage anemia
Tumor bleeding and renal involvement cause hematuria, urinary retention, anemia, pallor, and lethargy.
D
Irregular abdominal mass that characteristically crosses the midline
A midline-crossing irregular mass is typical of neuroblastoma rather than unilateral Wilms' tumor.
E
Carpopedal spasm and positive Chvostek's sign from hypocalcemia
Neuromuscular tetany is not a characteristic presenting feature of pediatric nephroblastoma.
q.obj: Wilms' tumor manifestations include a firm nontender unilateral flank mass, hematuria, urinary retention, anemia (pallor, lethargy), renin-induced hypertension, fever, and weight loss.
fc: Firm, nontender, unilateral mass deep in flank | Hypertension (excess renin secretion by tumor) | Hematuria, urinary retention, anemia (intratumoral hemorrhage), fever, weight loss

q.st: A 3-year-old child is hospitalized awaiting surgical resection of a suspected Wilms' tumor. Which preoperative nursing intervention is the highest priority for client safety?
o: A
Avoid palpating the abdomen and post a bedside sign reading 'Do Not Palpate Abdomen'
Palpating or handling the abdomen risks rupturing the encapsulated tumor and seeding cancer cells.
B
Palpate the flank mass every shift to monitor for rapid tumor enlargement
Abdominal palpation is strictly contraindicated because mechanical pressure can rupture the tumor capsule.
C
Perform deep abdominal percussion daily to assess for shifting ascites dullness
Percussion or manipulation of the abdomen can disrupt the tumor capsule and spread malignant cells.
D
Encourage rough-and-tumble play in the playroom to reduce preoperative anxiety
Physical trauma to the abdomen during active play risks rupturing the encapsulated renal tumor.
q.obj: Never palpate the abdomen of a child with Wilms' tumor; place a 'Do Not Palpate Abdomen' sign at the bedside to keep the encapsulated tumor intact.
fc: DO NOT palpate the abdomen; post 'Do Not Palpate Abdomen' sign | Handle/bathe carefully to keep encapsulated tumor intact | Tumor rupture spreads cancer cells to abdomen, lymph, and bloodstream
Ch. 32 Section III.C, Safety Alert & PQ 3

q.st: The nurse is caring for a 3-year-old child preoperatively with Wilms' tumor. How should the nurse safely monitor for changes in tumor size without risking tumor rupture?
o: A
Measure abdominal girth gently at least once daily
Measuring abdominal girth once daily noninvasively tracks abdominal enlargement without compressing the tumor.
B
Gently outline the tumor borders using firm fingertip palpation each morning
Fingertip palpation applies direct pressure to the tumor capsule and is strictly contraindicated.
C
Measure postvoid residual bladder volume using suprapubic ultrasound compression
Applying abdominal transducer pressure risks rupturing the fragile encapsulated nephroblastoma.
D
Weigh the child before and after every meal to detect tumor growth
Daily weight tracks fluid balance rather than safe noninvasive measurement of abdominal tumor expansion.
q.obj: Preoperative care for Wilms' tumor includes monitoring vital signs (especially blood pressure), avoiding abdominal palpation, and measuring abdominal girth at least once daily.
fc: Monitor vital signs, particularly blood pressure (renin hypertension) | Avoid palpation of the abdomen (bedside sign) | Measure abdominal girth at least once daily

q.st: A 4-year-old child returns to the pediatric unit following a total nephrectomy for Wilms' tumor. Which postoperative assessments are essential for detecting complications? Select all that apply.
o: A
Monitor strict intake and urine output closely to evaluate remaining renal function
After nephrectomy, strict intake and output monitoring verifies adequate function of the remaining kidney.
B
Assess bowel sounds and abdominal distention for signs of intestinal obstruction
Retroperitoneal surgery places the child at high postoperative risk for paralytic ileus or intestinal obstruction.
C
Monitor temperature, blood pressure, and signs of hemorrhage or infection
Close hemodynamic and temperature surveillance detects postoperative bleeding, infection, or blood pressure shifts.
D
Expect persistent severe hypertension caused by ongoing tumor renin secretion
Surgical removal of the renin-secreting tumor typically resolves tumor-induced hypertension postoperatively.
E
Keep the child NPO for 7 days regardless of returning bowel sounds
Diet is advanced once bowel sounds and gastrointestinal motility return rather than arbitrary prolonged fasting.
q.obj: Postoperative Wilms' tumor interventions include monitoring temperature, blood pressure, hemorrhage, infection, strict I&O, and bowel sounds/distention for intestinal obstruction.
fc: Monitor temperature, blood pressure, hemorrhage, and infection | Monitor strict intake and urine output closely | Monitor bowel sounds and abdominal distention (risk for intestinal obstruction)

q.st: A 3-year-old child diagnosed with Wilms' tumor develops new-onset dyspnea, shortness of breath, and chest pain. How should the nurse interpret these respiratory findings?
o: A
Potential pulmonary metastasis requiring immediate provider notification
Dyspnea, shortness of breath, and chest pain in Wilms' tumor indicate possible metastasis to the lungs.
B
Normal preoperative anxiety response common in preschool-age children
Chest pain and dyspnea are concerning indicators of lung metastasis rather than benign anxiety.
C
Expected side effect of preoperative renin-induced hypertension
Hypertension does not cause acute pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea without cardiopulmonary pathology.
D
Transient diaphragmatic spasm from daily abdominal girth measurement
Gentle abdominal girth measurement does not cause dyspnea or chest pain.
q.obj: In Wilms' tumor, symptoms of lung involvement such as dyspnea, shortness of breath, and chest pain indicate potential metastasis.
fc: Common metastatic site: lungs | Pulmonary cues: dyspnea, shortness of breath, chest pain | Treatment: combined surgery (partial/total nephrectomy) + chemo +/- radiation

q.st: A 2-year-old child is evaluated for a suspected neuroblastoma originating in the adrenal medulla. Which diagnostic urine test supports the diagnosis and monitors post-treatment response?
o: A
Urinary catecholamine breakdown products including vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid
Neuroblastoma tumors excrete elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid, homovanillic acid, dopamine, and norepinephrine.
B
24-hour urine collection for Bence Jones monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains
Bence Jones proteins are associated with adult multiple myeloma rather than pediatric neuroblastoma.
C
First-morning urine specimen for elevated phenylalanine metabolites
Urinary phenylpyruvic acid is associated with phenylketonuria rather than embryonic neural crest tumors.
D
Urine specific gravity and osmolality following water deprivation testing
Water deprivation testing evaluates diabetes insipidus rather than catecholamine-secreting neuroblastoma.
q.obj: Diagnostic evaluation for neuroblastoma includes analyzing urinary breakdown products: vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), homovanillic acid (HVA), dopamine, and norepinephrine.
fc: Originates from embryonic neural crest cells (adrenal medulla, sympathetic ganglia) | Most children present before age 10; often diagnosed after metastasis | Urine tests: VMA, homovanillic acid, dopamine, norepinephrine

q.st: The nurse is assessing a 3-year-old child admitted with metastatic neuroblastoma. Which clinical manifestations are characteristic of this tumor? Select all that apply.
o: A
Firm, nontender, irregular abdominal mass that crosses the midline
Unlike unilateral Wilms' tumor, an abdominal neuroblastoma characteristically crosses the midline.
B
Supraorbital ecchymosis, periorbital edema, and exophthalmos
Invasion of retrobulbar soft tissue produces characteristic periorbital bruising, edema, and eye protrusion.
C
Lower extremity weakness or paralysis from spinal cord compression
Paraspinal tumor extension can compress the spinal cord, causing neurological deficits and paralysis.
D
Smooth, encapsulated unilateral flank mass that never crosses the midline
A smooth, unilateral, encapsulated flank mass describes Wilms' tumor rather than irregular neuroblastoma.
E
Painless, movable left supraclavicular 'sentinel' node with Reed-Sternberg cells
Reed-Sternberg cells in a left supraclavicular node characterize Hodgkin's lymphoma rather than neuroblastoma.
q.obj: Neuroblastoma cues include a firm irregular midline-crossing abdominal mass, urinary frequency/retention, cervical/supraclavicular nodes, bone pain, periorbital ecchymosis/exophthalmos, and cord paralysis.
fc: Firm, nontender, irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline | Supraorbital ecchymosis, periorbital edema, exophthalmos (retrobulbar invasion) | Urinary frequency/retention, bone pain, respiratory/neuro signs, spinal cord paralysis

q.st: The parents of a 4-year-old child newly diagnosed with stage IV neuroblastoma ask why the prognosis is guarded. Which factor primarily explains the poor overall prognosis of neuroblastoma?
o: A
The tumor is highly invasive and most diagnoses are not made until after metastasis occurs
Frequent invasiveness and late diagnosis after metastasis contribute to the poor prognosis in neuroblastoma.
B
Neuroblastoma cells are completely resistant to all radiation and chemotherapy agents
Radiation provides palliation and chemotherapy treats disseminated disease, though metastasis limits cure.
C
Children diagnosed under 1 year of age have the lowest survival rates
The younger the child at diagnosis, the better the survival rate in neuroblastoma.
D
Surgical biopsy causes immediate fatal catecholamine hypertensive crisis in all cases
Surgical biopsy and resection are standard diagnostic and therapeutic procedures rather than universally fatal.
q.obj: Neuroblastoma prognosis is poor because of tumor invasiveness and diagnosis after metastasis; however, the younger the child at diagnosis, the better the survival rate.
fc: Prognosis poor due to invasiveness and diagnosis after metastasis | Younger age at diagnosis = better survival rate | Early stage: complete surgical removal; Late stage: biopsy, palliative radiation, chemo

q.st: During postoperative care for a 3-year-old child who underwent biopsy of an advanced metastatic neuroblastoma, the parents tearfully state, 'We feel so guilty that we did not notice these signs sooner.' Which nursing response is most therapeutic?
o: A
Encourage them to express their feelings and reassure them that early signs are often silent until metastasis
Many parents feel guilt for missing signs; encouraging emotional expression and offering support is essential.
B
Remind them that earlier pediatric checkups would have prevented metastatic spread
Blaming parents intensifies overwhelming guilt and is nontherapeutic during a devastating diagnosis.
C
Change the subject immediately to postoperative vital signs to distract them from crying
Avoiding parental grief prevents therapeutic processing and emotional adjustment to the child's illness.
D
Tell them not to worry because neuroblastoma is always cured with palliative radiation
Offering false reassurance undermines trust; later-stage radiation provides palliation rather than guaranteed cure.
q.obj: Postoperatively, the nurse provides emotional support to parents of children with neuroblastoma, encouraging them to express feelings and addressing parental guilt.
fc: Monitor organ-specific postoperative complications and chemo/radiation effects | Encourage parents to express feelings (many feel guilt for not recognizing signs earlier) | Refer parents to appropriate community services

q.st: A 2-year-old child with a retroperitoneal neuroblastoma compressing the lumbar spine suddenly stops moving both legs and has urinary retention. Which priority action should the nurse take?
o: A
Notify the primary health care provider immediately of suspected spinal cord compression
New lower extremity paralysis indicates acute spinal cord compression from tumor extension requiring urgent intervention.
B
Encourage the toddler to walk in the hallway to prevent muscle atrophy
Ambulation is impossible with acute paralysis and risks falls and spinal injury.
C
Document the finding as expected fatigue following chemotherapy administration
Acute paralysis is a neurological emergency rather than generalized chemotherapy-induced fatigue.
D
Apply warm compresses to the lower extremities and reassess in 4 hours
Delaying notification during acute spinal cord compression risks permanent irreversible paralysis.
q.obj: Neuroblastoma can cause paralysis from compression of the spinal cord and urinary frequency or retention from urinary tract compression.
fc: Most signs result from tumor compressing adjacent normal organs | Spinal cord compression -> paralysis (neurological emergency) | Kidney/ureter/bladder compression -> urinary frequency or retention

q.st: The nurse conducts an educational session for pediatric nurses on osteosarcoma. Which statement by a staff nurse indicates a need for further instruction?
o: A
The child does not experience pain at the primary tumor site
Osteosarcoma causes progressive localized pain at the tumor site, often initially mistaken for growing pains.
B
The femur is the most common anatomical site of this sarcoma
Osteosarcoma typically arises in the metaphysis of lower extremity long bones, most commonly the femur.
C
Limping is a clinical manifestation when a weight-bearing limb is affected
Pain and mass in a lower extremity commonly produce a limp and curtailed physical activity.
D
Early-stage symptoms are almost always attributed to injury or normal growing pains
Early localized bone pain is frequently misattributed to sports trauma or normal adolescent growing pains.
q.obj: Osteosarcoma (most common childhood bone cancer; peak age 13-16) occurs most often in the distal femur metaphysis and causes localized pain, limping, and pathological fractures.
fc: Most common bone cancer in children; peak age 13-16 | Most common site: metaphysis of long bones, especially femur | Manifestations: localized pain (relieved by flexed position), palpable mass, limp, fractures

q.st: A 15-year-old adolescent is evaluated for persistent right distal thigh pain and swelling that has worsened over 2 months. Which assessment findings support a suspected diagnosis of osteosarcoma? Select all that apply.
o: A
Localized bone pain relieved by holding the extremity in a flexed position
Pain in osteosarcoma is typically localized to the metaphysis and partially relieved by limb flexion.
B
Palpable mass with progressive limited range of motion and limping
Tumor expansion creates a palpable mass, restricts joint motion, and causes limping in weight-bearing limbs.
C
Inability to hold heavy objects and occurrence of pathological fractures
Cortical bone destruction weakens the limb, causing pain with weight bearing and pathological fractures.
D
Painless, freely movable cervical lymphadenopathy with night sweats
Painless cervical adenopathy and night sweats characterize Hodgkin's disease rather than osteosarcoma.
E
Hypertension and hematuria accompanied by a unilateral flank mass
Hypertension, hematuria, and a flank mass indicate Wilms' tumor rather than primary bone sarcoma.
q.obj: Osteosarcoma assessment reveals localized pain (often relieved by flexion), palpable mass, limping, limited ROM, inability to hold heavy objects, and pathological fractures.
fc: Localized pain at affected site (often relieved by flexed position) | Palpable mass, limping, progressive limited ROM, curtailed activity | Inability to hold heavy objects; pathological fractures at tumor site

q.st: A 14-year-old adolescent scheduled for an above-the-knee amputation for femoral osteosarcoma expresses distress about losing the leg and asks what phantom limb pain feels like. How should the nurse explain phantom limb pain?
o: A
It is a tingling, itching, and painful sensation felt in the area where the limb was amputated
Phantom limb pain is characterized by tingling, itching, and pain perceived in the amputated limb area.
B
It is a psychological hallucination caused by preoperative chemotherapy medications
Phantom limb pain is a real neuropathic sensation originating from severed peripheral nerves rather than hallucination.
C
It only occurs if the surgical incision becomes infected after prosthetic fitting
Phantom limb sensations can occur after any amputation regardless of surgical wound infection.
D
It indicates local recurrence of osteosarcoma inside the remaining stump
Phantom limb pain is an expected post-amputation phenomenon rather than proof of tumor recurrence.
q.obj: Preoperative amputation teaching includes honest communication, self-image support, prosthetic preparation, and explaining phantom limb pain (tingling, itching, and pain in the amputated area).
fc: Treatment: limb salvage resection or amputation + pre/post-op chemotherapy | Support adolescent self-image and prepare for prosthetic fitting | Teach phantom limb pain: tingling, itching, and pain in amputated area

q.st: A 15-year-old client with osteosarcoma of the left distal femur is awaiting neoadjuvant chemotherapy and limb-salvage surgery. Which nursing intervention is most important to prevent injury?
o: A
Instruct the adolescent to avoid weight-bearing on the affected leg and use crutches as prescribed
Tumor invasion weakens the femur, placing the adolescent at high risk for a pathological fracture.
B
Encourage daily jogging and stair climbing to maintain quadriceps muscle strength
High-impact weight-bearing activity on a tumor-weakened femur can precipitate an acute pathological fracture.
C
Perform vigorous passive hip and knee stretching exercises every shift
Forceful passive manipulation of the affected bone risks causing a pathological fracture at the tumor site.
D
Apply tight elastic compression wraps to force the knee into full extension
Forcing full extension increases pain (often relieved by flexion) and risks neurovascular compromise.
q.obj: Because pathological fractures occur at the osteosarcoma tumor site, the affected extremity must be protected from trauma and weight-bearing stress.
fc: Pathological fractures occur at the primary metaphyseal tumor site | Protect affected extremity from weight-bearing stress and trauma | Communicate honestly and support adolescent body image

q.st: An 8-year-old child is diagnosed with an infratentorial brain tumor. Which anatomical location and clinical presentation are most characteristic of infratentorial tumors in children?
o: A
Located in the cerebellum or brainstem (posterior third), frequently causing increased ICP and ataxia
Infratentorial tumors are the most common pediatric brain tumors and frequently cause increased ICP and ataxia.
B
Located in the anterior cerebral cortex, rarely causing symptoms of increased intracranial pressure
Anterior cerebral tumors are supratentorial, whereas posterior fossa infratentorial tumors commonly cause ICP.
C
Located exclusively in the lumbar spinal canal, causing isolated lower extremity flaccidity
Infratentorial tumors reside below the tentorium cerebelli in the cerebellum or brainstem rather than lumbar spine.
D
Located in the adrenal medulla, causing catecholamine-induced episodic hypertension
Adrenal medullary tumors describe neuroblastoma rather than infratentorial pediatric brain tumors.
q.obj: Infratentorial tumors (below the tentorium cerebelli, in the cerebellum/brainstem) are the most common pediatric brain tumors and frequently cause increased ICP.
fc: Infratentorial (most common): posterior third (cerebellum/brainstem) -> high ICP risk | Supratentorial: anterior two-thirds (cerebrum) | Most common diagnostic procedure: MRI

q.st: The nurse is assessing a 7-year-old child with a suspected cerebellar brain tumor. Which clinical manifestations are characteristic of pediatric brain tumors? Select all that apply.
o: A
Headache that is worse upon awakening and improves during the day
Recumbent sleeping increases intracranial venous pressure, making brain tumor headaches worst upon morning awakening.
B
Vomiting that is unrelated to feeding or eating
Direct medullary vomiting center stimulation causes sudden vomiting unrelated to meals or nausea.
C
Ataxia, clumsiness, awkward gait, diplopia, and facial weakness
Cerebellar and brainstem compression produce gait ataxia, clumsiness, diplopia, and cranial nerve weakness.
D
Localized distal femur pain relieved by knee flexion
Localized distal femur pain describes osteosarcoma rather than an intracranial neoplasm.
E
Painless unilateral flank mass accompanied by hematuria
A unilateral flank mass with hematuria indicates Wilms' tumor rather than a cerebellar brain tumor.
q.obj: Pediatric brain tumor cues include morning headache improving during the day, vomiting unrelated to eating, ataxia, seizures, behavioral changes, clumsiness, diplopia, and facial weakness.
fc: Headache worse on awakening, improves during day; vomiting unrelated to eating | Ataxia, clumsiness, awkward gait, diplopia, facial weakness | Seizures and behavioral changes; notify PHCP immediately if ICP signs occur

q.st: The nurse is preparing a 6-year-old child for a craniotomy to resect a brain tumor. Which preoperative nursing interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: A
Perform neurological assessments at least every 4 hours and institute seizure precautions
Frequent baseline neurological checks and seizure precautions detect deterioration and prevent injury.
B
Prepare the child for waking up with a large head dressing and provide a favorite cap
Age-appropriate preparation for head shaving and a bulky dressing reduces postoperative fear.
C
Assess baseline weight loss and nutritional status
Evaluating nutritional status and weight loss identifies preoperative deficits requiring support.
D
Administer a preoperative cleansing enema to reduce intracranial pressure
Enemas increase intra-abdominal and intracranial pressure and are avoided before craniotomy.
E
Place the child in Trendelenburg position overnight to promote cerebral perfusion
Trendelenburg position elevates intracranial pressure and is strictly contraindicated before or after craniotomy.
q.obj: Preoperative craniotomy care includes neurological checks every 4 hours, seizure precautions, nutritional assessment, head-shaving preparation with a favorite cap, and dressing teaching.
fc: Perform neurological assessment at least every 4 hours | Institute seizure precautions and safety measures; assess weight/nutrition | Provide favorite cap/hat after head shave; prepare child for large head dressing

q.st: While checking the head dressing of a child 4 hours after craniotomy for brain tumor removal, the nurse notes a ring of colorless drainage on the back of the dressing. Which action should the nurse perform immediately?
o: A
Notify the surgeon immediately
Colorless drainage indicates cerebrospinal fluid leakage, risking meningitis and herniation, requiring immediate surgeon notification.
B
Reinforce the dressing with sterile gauze and reassess in 2 hours
Reinforcing without notifying the surgeon delays urgent intervention for an active cerebrospinal fluid leak.
C
Remove the entire surgical head dressing to inspect the underlying suture line
Nurses must never change or remove a craniotomy dressing without a specific surgeon prescription.
D
Circle the colorless drainage with a pen and document it as normal serous exudate
Colorless cranial or ear/nose drainage represents cerebrospinal fluid (test for glucose) rather than benign exudate.
q.obj: Colorless drainage on a craniotomy dressing or from the ears/nose indicates cerebrospinal fluid (positive for glucose) and must be reported to the surgeon immediately.
fc: Colorless drainage on dressing, ears, or nose = CSF leak (test with glucose dipstick) | Action: notify the surgeon IMMEDIATELY | Check back of dressing for blood pooling; mark edges; DO NOT change dressing without order

q.st: During the postoperative period following surgical removal of a brain tumor, a child becomes restless with an elevated pulse rate and a markedly decreased blood pressure from baseline. Suspecting shock, what is the nurse's most appropriate action?
o: A
Notify the surgeon immediately
Suspected postoperative shock requires immediate surgeon notification while avoiding ICP-elevating positions or fluid boluses.
B
Place the child in Trendelenburg's position to restore cerebral blood pressure
Trendelenburg's position dangerously increases intracranial pressure and hemorrhage risk after craniotomy.
C
Rapidly increase the intravenous fluid infusion rate to 200 mL/hr
Increasing intravenous fluid rates without a prescription can precipitate life-threatening cerebral edema and ICP.
D
Lower the head of the bed to a completely flat supine position
Lowering a post-craniotomy child supine can increase intracranial pressure; the surgeon must be notified immediately.
q.obj: If shock is suspected after craniotomy, notify the surgeon immediately; never use Trendelenburg's position or increase IV fluids unprescribed, which elevate ICP.
fc: Suspected shock (restlessness, tachycardia, falling BP) -> notify surgeon IMMEDIATELY | NEVER place in Trendelenburg's position (increases ICP and bleeding) | NEVER increase IV fluid rate without prescription (worsens cerebral edema)

q.st: The nurse is reviewing postoperative positioning prescriptions for children recovering from craniotomy procedures. Which positioning principles are correct? Select all that apply.
o: A
After supratentorial surgery, elevate the head above heart level to promote CSF drainage
Head elevation above heart level facilitates cerebrospinal fluid drainage and reduces cerebral blood flow.
B
After infratentorial surgery, position the child flat or on either side as prescribed
Infratentorial craniotomies typically require flat or side-lying positioning rather than high head elevation.
C
Never place the child on the operative side if a large tumor was removed
Turning onto the operative cavity after large tumor removal can cause sudden dangerous brain shift.
D
Place the child in Trendelenburg's position to prevent postoperative orthostatic hypotension
Trendelenburg's position is strictly contraindicated because it raises intracranial pressure and hemorrhage risk.
E
Flex the child's chin tightly onto the chest to stabilize the cervical spine
Extreme neck flexion obstructs jugular venous outflow and increases intracranial pressure.
q.obj: Post-craniotomy positioning: follow surgeon's neck flexion order; never use Trendelenburg; avoid operative side if large tumor removed; flat/side-lying for infratentorial; head elevated for supratentorial.
fc: Supratentorial: head elevated above heart level (promotes CSF drainage, decreases bleeding) | Infratentorial: flat or on either side | Never Trendelenburg; do not place on operative side if large tumor removed

q.st: A child recovering from brainstem tumor resection develops a temperature of 39.6 C (103.3 F) 6 hours postoperatively despite clean surgical dressings and clear lungs. What is the most likely physiological cause of this fever?
o: A
Hypothalamic or brainstem temperature-regulation disturbance caused by surgical manipulation
Hypothalamus or brainstem involvement during surgery causes central hyperthermia, requiring a bedside cooling blanket.
B
Late-onset surgical wound cellulitis requiring immediate dressing removal
Surgical wound infections rarely develop within 6 hours, and dressings are not removed without orders.
C
Anaphylactic reaction to preoperative head shaving soap
Anaphylaxis presents with bronchospasm and hypotension rather than isolated central postoperative hyperthermia.
D
Expected thermogenic response to postoperative fasting and fluid restriction
Fasting does not cause a high fever of 39.6 C; central thermoregulatory disruption is responsible.
q.obj: Post-craniotomy temperature may become elevated from hypothalamus or brainstem involvement during surgery; maintain a cooling blanket at the bedside.
fc: Monitor temperature closely (may rise from hypothalamus/brainstem surgical involvement) | Maintain a cooling blanket by the bedside | Also monitor for respiratory infection and meningitis (opisthotonos, Kernig's, Brudzinski's)

q.st: The nurse is monitoring a child 12 hours after craniotomy for neurological complications. Which findings require immediate reporting to the primary health care provider? Select all that apply.
o: A
Sluggish, dilated, or unequal pupils
Pupillary asymmetry or sluggish reactivity signals rising intracranial pressure and impending brainstem herniation.
B
Opisthotonos with positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs
Nuchal rigidity, opisthotonos, and positive Kernig's/Brudzinski's signs indicate acute postoperative meningitis.
C
Persistent retching and forceful vomiting
Vomiting sharply elevates intracranial pressure and places the child at risk for incisional rupture.
D
Alert orientation with equal 3 mm briskly reactive pupils
Alert mental status and briskly reactive equal pupils reflect stable postoperative neurological recovery.
E
Sleeping quietly in a dim room between scheduled neurological assessments
Resting calmly in a quiet environment helps prevent agitation-induced spikes in intracranial pressure.
q.obj: Post-craniotomy, immediately report sluggish/dilated/unequal pupils (herniation), meningitis signs (opisthotonos, Kernig's, Brudzinski's), increased ICP, and prevent vomiting.
fc: Sluggish, dilated, or unequal pupils -> report immediately (ICP/brainstem herniation) | Meningitis signs: opisthotonos, Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs | Prevent vomiting (increases ICP and risk for incisional rupture)

q.st: A parent calls the pediatric triage clinic reporting that their 3-week-old newborn has a rectal temperature of 38.2 C (100.8 F) and is feeding poorly. Which instruction should the nurse provide immediately?
o: A
Bring the infant for immediate medical evaluation because fever under 1 month is an emergency
Fever in an infant under 1 month old is an emergency requiring immediate evaluation.
B
Administer weight-based children's ibuprofen and recheck the temperature in 4 hours
Ibuprofen is not given under 6 months, and neonatal fever requires immediate emergency evaluation.
C
Give a cool water sponge bath at home and call back tomorrow if fever persists
Neonates with fever >= 38.0 C require immediate evaluation for sepsis rather than home observation.
D
Administer half a baby aspirin dissolved in formula to lower the temperature quickly
Aspirin is contraindicated in children due to Reye's syndrome, and neonatal fever is an emergency.
q.obj: Normal pediatric temperature is 36.4 C to 37.0 C (97.5 F to 98.6 F); fever is >=38.0 C (100.4 F), and fever in an infant <1 month old is an emergency.
fc: Normal child temp: 36.4-37.0 C (97.5-98.6 F); Fever: >= 38.0 C (100.4 F) | Fever in infant < 1 month old = EMERGENCY -> contact pediatrician immediately | Signs: flushed warm skin, diaphoresis, chills, restlessness/lethargy

q.st: The nurse has just administered a prescribed dose of ibuprofen to a 2-year-old child with a temperature of 38.8 C (102.0 F). Which nursing action should the nurse implement next?
o: A
Remove excess clothing and blankets and increase room air circulation
Removing excess coverings promotes heat dissipation through evaporation and radiation without inducing shivering.
B
Sponge-bathe the child with ice-cold water to drop the temperature rapidly
Cold water sponging induces shivering, which increases metabolic oxygen demand and raises core temperature.
C
Withhold all oral fluids for 6 hours to prevent fever-induced vomiting
Fever increases insensible fluid losses, requiring adequate oral fluid intake to prevent dehydration.
D
Administer a dose of oral aspirin in 2 hours if the temperature remains elevated
Aspirin must never be administered to febrile children due to the risk of Reye's syndrome.
q.obj: Fever interventions include removing excess clothing/blankets, cooling the room, giving acetaminophen or ibuprofen (>6 months), avoiding aspirin (Reye's syndrome), and encouraging fluids.
fc: Remove excess clothing/blankets; reduce room temp; cool compress to forehead | Antipyretics: acetaminophen or ibuprofen (> 6 months); NO aspirin (Reye's syndrome) | Retake temperature 30-60 min after antipyretic; encourage fluids

q.st: The nurse administers oral acetaminophen to a 4-year-old child with a temperature of 39.1 C (102.4 F). When should the nurse retake the child's temperature to evaluate medication effectiveness?
o: A
30 to 60 minutes after administering the antipyretic
Retaking the temperature 30 to 60 minutes post-administration accurately evaluates antipyretic therapeutic response.
B
5 minutes after administering the oral suspension
Five minutes is insufficient for gastrointestinal absorption and hypothalamic thermoregulatory onset.
C
4 hours after administering the antipyretic
Waiting 4 hours delays recognition of persistent hyperthermia or need for alternative cooling measures.
D
Only if the child develops visible febrile seizure activity
Scheduled reassessment 30 to 60 minutes after dosing is standard nursing evaluation practice.
q.obj: After administering an antipyretic to a febrile child, the nurse should retake the temperature 30 to 60 minutes later.
fc: Retake temperature 30 to 60 minutes after antipyretic administration | Monitor for dehydration and electrolyte imbalances | Teach parents safe dosing and when to call PHCP

q.st: A parent asks the pediatric nurse why aspirin should not be given to lower a child's fever during a viral respiratory illness. What is the nurse's best explanation?
o: A
Administering aspirin to a child with a viral fever carries a risk of Reye's syndrome
Aspirin is avoided in febrile children unless specifically prescribed due to Reye's syndrome risk.
B
Aspirin causes severe irreversible tooth staining in children under 8 years old
Tooth discoloration is associated with tetracycline antibiotics rather than pediatric salicylate administration.
C
Aspirin triggers acute adrenal crisis and severe neonatal hyperkalemia
The specific life-threatening complication linked to pediatric aspirin use during fever is Reye's syndrome.
D
Aspirin is completely ineffective at reducing hypothalamic fever set points in children
Aspirin reduces fever pharmacologically but is contraindicated because of Reye's syndrome toxicity.
q.obj: Aspirin is not administered to children with fever unless specifically prescribed because of the risk of Reye's syndrome.
fc: Never administer aspirin to a febrile child unless specifically prescribed | Reason: risk of Reye's syndrome (acute encephalopathy + fatty liver) | Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen (> 6 months old) instead

q.st: A mother brings her 4-month-old infant with a temperature of 38.5 C (101.3 F) to the clinic and asks if she can give over-the-counter infant ibuprofen. Which guidance should the nurse provide?
o: A
Ibuprofen is only given to infants older than 6 months; use prescribed acetaminophen instead
Ibuprofen is approved for febrile infants and children older than 6 months of age.
B
Ibuprofen is safe at any age starting at birth as long as liquid drops are used
Ibuprofen should not be administered until the infant is older than 6 months.
C
Alternate aspirin and ibuprofen every 2 hours until the fever resolves
Both aspirin (Reye's syndrome) and ibuprofen (<6 months) are inappropriate for a 4-month-old infant.
D
Bundle the infant in two warm blankets to sweat out the viral fever
Bundling traps body heat and worsens hyperthermia; excess clothing should be removed.
q.obj: For pediatric fever, administer antipyretics such as acetaminophen or, if the child is older than 6 months, ibuprofen as prescribed.
fc: Acetaminophen: appropriate across pediatric ages as prescribed | Ibuprofen: administer ONLY if child is older than 6 months | Aspirin: contraindicated due to Reye's syndrome

q.st: The nurse is explaining to parents why infants and young children develop dehydration much more rapidly than adults during gastroenteritis. Which physiological factor accounts for this heightened vulnerability?
o: A
Infants and children have immature water-conserving organs and more body water in the extracellular compartment
Immature renal conservation and a larger extracellular fluid proportion predispose children to rapid fluid deficit.
B
Infants and children have smaller body surface area relative to weight and low metabolic rates
Infants have greater body surface area and higher metabolic rates, accelerating insensible fluid losses.
C
Infants store 90% of total body water inside bone and adipose tissue
A higher proportion of pediatric body water resides in the labile extracellular fluid compartment.
D
Infants excrete concentrated urine with a baseline specific gravity above 1.040
Immature neonatal kidneys have limited concentrating ability, increasing obligatory urinary water losses.
q.obj: Infants and children are more vulnerable to fluid volume deficit because water-conserving organs are immature and more body water is in the extracellular fluid compartment.
fc: Water-conserving organs (kidneys) are immature in infants/children | More body water is located in the extracellular fluid (ECF) compartment | Causes: fever, poor intake, vomiting, diarrhea, DKA, extensive burns

q.st: An 8-month-old infant weighing 10 kg before illness is admitted with acute diarrhea and now weighs 9.3 kg (7% weight loss). Assessment shows dry mucous membranes, decreased tears, capillary refill of 3 seconds, and urine specific gravity of 1.026. Which level of dehydration is present?
o: A
Moderate dehydration
Infant weight loss of 6% to 9% with dry mucosa indicates moderate dehydration.
B
Mild dehydration
Mild dehydration in infants presents with 3% to 5% weight loss, normal mucosa, and present tears.
C
Severe dehydration
Severe infant dehydration involves >=10% weight loss, parched mucosa, absent tears, and refill >4 seconds.
D
Normal hydration status
A 7% acute weight loss with delayed capillary refill reflects significant moderate fluid volume deficit.
q.obj: Moderate dehydration in infants features 6%-9% weight loss (6%-8% in children), slightly increased pulse, slight tachypnea, dry mucosa, decreased tears, and 2-4 sec capillary refill.
fc: Weight loss: 6%-9% (infants), 6%-8% (children) | Dry mucous membranes, decreased tears, irritable, moderate thirst | Capillary refill 2-4 sec, urine specific gravity > 1.020 with oliguria

q.st: The nurse is assessing a toddler admitted with severe gastroenteritis and suspected severe dehydration (10% body weight loss). Which clinical findings confirm severe dehydration? Select all that apply.
o: A
Very delayed capillary refill (>4 seconds) with skin tenting and cool, mottled skin
Profound peripheral vasoconstriction in severe dehydration prolongs capillary refill beyond 4 seconds with mottling.
B
Parched mucous membranes, absent tears, sunken eyes, and sunken anterior fontanel
Severe extracellular and interstitial depletion causes parched mucosa, absent tears, and sunken eyes/fontanel.
C
Hyperpnea (deep, rapid respirations), marked tachycardia, and orthostatic hypotension to shock
Metabolic acidosis and hypovolemic shock trigger Kussmaul-like hyperpnea, severe tachycardia, and falling blood pressure.
D
Normal capillary refill of 2 seconds with present tears and moist mucosa
Two-second capillary refill and present tears characterize mild dehydration rather than severe shock.
E
External jugular vein clearly visible when the child is placed supine
In severe dehydration, the external jugular vein is not visible even with supraclavicular pressure.
