q.obj: Severe dehydration (>=10% infant/10% child weight loss) causes marked tachycardia, hyperpnea, shock, lethargy, intense thirst, parched mucosa, absent tears, sunken eyes/fontanel, and refill >4 sec.
fc: Weight loss: >= 10% (infants), 10% (children); oliguria/anuria | Parched mucosa, absent tears, sunken eyes/fontanel, skin tenting/mottled | Very increased pulse, hyperpnea, shock, capillary refill > 4 sec

q.st: A 14-month-old toddler is admitted with hypernatremic dehydration (serum sodium 156 mEq/L). Why must the nurse exercise extra caution when evaluating skin turgor and mucous membranes in this child?
o: A
Classic skin tenting and dry mucous membrane signs are less prominent in hypernatremic dehydration
Clinical signs of dehydration in Table 33.1 are less prominent in a child with hypernatremia.
B
Hypernatremia always causes severe generalized pitting edema that masks weight loss
Hypernatremic dehydration causes intracellular water loss rather than generalized pitting fluid overload.
C
Serum sodium elevation artificially shortens capillary refill to less than 1 second
Hypernatremia preserves intravascular volume temporarily, making skin turgor signs less reliable.
D
Hypernatremic children never develop oliguria or elevated urinary specific gravity
Hypernatremic children conserve water with oliguria, though cutaneous dehydration signs appear milder.
q.obj: Physical signs of dehydration (such as poor skin turgor and tenting) are less prominent in a child who has hypernatremia, potentially masking dehydration severity.
fc: Table 33.1 physical signs are LESS prominent in hypernatremia | Intracellular water shifts into vessels, masking skin tenting | Monitor weight, I&O, neurological status, and electrolytes closely

q.st: The parents of a 2-year-old child with mild diarrhea and dehydration ask which fluids to offer at home for oral rehydration therapy. Which fluid recommendation should the nurse provide?
o: A
Offer frequent small amounts of an oral rehydration solution such as Pedialyte
Oral rehydration solutions like Pedialyte replace water and electrolytes in balanced physiological proportions.
B
Give chilled apple juice to provide extra glucose energy during diarrhea
High-sugar fluids like apple juice exert an osmotic effect that worsens diarrhea and dehydration.
C
Offer flat ginger ale or carbonated lemon-lime soda throughout the day
Carbonated beverages are gas-producing, high in sugar, and low in electrolytes, worsening diarrhea.
D
Administer plain distilled water exclusively for 48 hours until stools firm up
Plain water lacks sodium and potassium and can precipitate dilutional hyponatremia in dehydrated children.
q.obj: For mild to moderate dehydration, provide oral rehydration therapy with Pedialyte or similar solutions; avoid carbonated beverages (gas-producing) and high-sugar fluids like apple juice.
fc: Use Pedialyte or similar prescribed oral rehydration solution | AVOID carbonated beverages (gas-producing) | AVOID high-sugar fluids such as apple juice (worsens osmotic diarrhea)

q.st: A pediatrician prescribes an intravenous infusion of 5% dextrose and 0.45% sodium chloride with 40 mEq of potassium chloride for a child with hypotonic dehydration. Which priority assessment must the nurse perform before starting this infusion?
o: A
Verify that the child has voided and has adequate urine output
Intravenous potassium must never be administered until adequate renal function and voiding are confirmed.
B
Obtain an axillary temperature to rule out concurrent viral fever
Assessing temperature is routine care but is not the critical safety check before potassium infusion.
C
Measure head circumference and anterior fontanel tension
Fontanel assessment evaluates intracranial pressure rather than renal clearance of intravenous potassium.
D
Check capillary blood glucose to confirm absence of hypoglycemia
Confirming adequate urine output (>= 1-2 mL/kg/hr) is the mandatory priority before infusing potassium.
q.obj: If potassium is prescribed for IV administration in dehydration, the nurse must ensure the child has voided first and has adequate renal function.
fc: IV Potassium Safety in Pediatric Dehydration (PQ 3)

Severe dehydration: NPO to rest bowel + IV fluid/electrolyte replacement | PRIORITY before IV potassium: ensure child has VOIDED and has adequate renal function | Never give IV potassium during oliguria or anuria (fatal hyperkalemia)

q.st: A child admitted with moderate fluid volume deficit has received 6 hours of rehydration therapy. Which assessment finding indicates that the child is improving and the fluid deficit is resolving?
o: A
Capillary refill is less than 2 seconds
A capillary refill time under 2 seconds indicates restored peripheral perfusion and resolving dehydration.
B
Urine specific gravity is 1.035
A specific gravity of 1.035 exceeds the normal 1.003-1.030 range and indicates persistent dehydration.
C
Urine output is 0.5 mL/kg/hr
Adequate pediatric urine output is at least 1 mL/kg/hr; 0.5 mL/kg/hr indicates ongoing oliguria.
D
Absence of tears when crying
Lack of tears reflects persistent moderate-to-severe extracellular fluid depletion rather than resolving dehydration.
q.obj: Indicators of resolving pediatric fluid volume deficit include capillary refill <2 seconds, urine specific gravity 1.003-1.030, urine output >=1 mL/kg/hr, and adequate tear production.
fc: Capillary refill < 2 seconds | Urine output >= 1 mL/kg/hr and urine specific gravity 1.003 to 1.030 | Adequate tear production and moist mucous membranes; reintroduce normal diet once rehydrated

q.st: A 9-month-old infant is admitted with mild dehydration secondary to decreased oral intake. Which clinical finding in Table 33.1 is consistent with mild dehydration?
o: A
Weight loss of 3% to 5%, present tears, normal mucous membranes, and urine specific gravity >1.020
Mild infant dehydration exhibits 3%-5% weight loss, normal mucosa, present tears, and concentrated urine >1.020.
B
Weight loss of 8%, sunken anterior fontanel, and delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds
An 8% weight loss with sunken fontanel and delayed refill represents moderate-to-severe dehydration.
C
Weight loss of 12%, anuria, mottled cool skin, and orthostatic shock
Twelve percent weight loss with anuria and shock represents severe life-threatening dehydration.
D
External jugular vein invisible even when supraclavicular pressure is applied
Invisible external jugular veins under supraclavicular pressure indicate severe intravascular volume depletion.
q.obj: Mild dehydration involves 3%-5% infant (3%-4% child) weight loss, normal pulse/respirations/BP/mucosa, present tears, slight thirst, 2-sec refill, and urine specific gravity >1.020.
fc: Weight loss: 3%-5% (infants), 3%-4% (children) | Normal pulse, RR, BP, behavior, mucous membranes; tears present | Slight thirst, capillary refill 2 sec, urine specific gravity > 1.020

q.st: A parent brings a 2-week-old infant to the clinic for a repeat phenylketonuria (PKU) blood test, which shows a serum phenylalanine level of 1.0 mg/dL (60.5 mcmol/L). How should the nurse interpret this result?
o: A
Negative test result within the normal reference range of 0 to 2 mg/dL
Normal serum phenylalanine is 0 to 2 mg/dL; levels >20 mg/dL indicate phenylketonuria.
B
Positive diagnostic result confirming classic autosomal recessive phenylketonuria
A diagnostic positive PKU result requires a blood phenylalanine level exceeding 20 mg/dL.
C
Inconclusive specimen requiring immediate initiation of phenylalanine-free formula
A level of 1.0 mg/dL is normal and negative, requiring no dietary protein restriction.
D
Borderline elevation requiring repeat heel-stick testing at 6 months of age
Because 1.0 mg/dL is within the normal 0-2 mg/dL range, no further rescreening is needed.
q.obj: Normal serum phenylalanine is 0 to 2 mg/dL (0 to 121 mcmol/L); phenylketonuria is characterized by blood phenylalanine levels greater than 20 mg/dL (1210 mcmol/L).
fc: Autosomal recessive disorder causing CNS damage from toxic phenylalanine | Normal serum phenylalanine: 0 to 2 mg/dL (0 to 121 mcmol/L) | Diagnostic PKU level: > 20 mg/dL (1210 mcmol/L)

q.st: The nurse is preparing to collect a newborn screening blood specimen for phenylketonuria (PKU) prior to hospital discharge. Which pre-collection requirement and follow-up rule are essential for accurate screening?
o: A
Ensure the infant has begun formula or human milk feedings, and rescreen by 14 days if tested before 24 hours
Protein intake from milk/formula is required for phenylalanine accumulation, and early tests (<24 hr) need rescreening.
B
Collect the heel-stick blood specimen immediately after birth before the first feeding
Testing before protein ingestion produces false-negative results because phenylalanine has not yet accumulated.
C
Keep the newborn NPO on sterile water for 12 hours prior to capillary blood collection
Fasting prevents dietary protein metabolism and invalidates newborn phenylketonuria screening.
D
Delay initial newborn screening until 6 weeks of age in all 50 states
All 50 states mandate newborn screening prior to discharge, with rescreening by 14 days if early.
q.obj: For PKU screening, the newborn must have begun formula or human milk feedings before specimen collection, and infants tested before 24 hours of age must be rescreened by 14 days.
fc: Required in all 50 states; infant must receive formula or human milk first | Rescreen by 14 days of age if initial screen was done before 24 hours | Positive initial screen requires repeat test and diagnostic evaluation

q.st: The nurse is assessing an untreated 2-year-old child recently adopted from a region without newborn screening who is diagnosed with phenylketonuria (PKU). Which clinical manifestations are associated with untreated PKU? Select all that apply.
o: A
Musty odor of the urine, vomiting, and intellectual disability
Accumulated phenylacetic acid produces a musty urine odor alongside vomiting, seizures, and intellectual disability.
B
Eczema, hypertonia, and hypopigmentation of the hair, skin, and irises
Impaired tyrosine melanin synthesis in older untreated children causes fair hair, light skin/irises, eczema, and hypertonia.
C
Seizures and behavioral abnormalities including hyperactivity or bizarre behavior
Toxic blood phenylalanine damages the developing brain, causing seizures and severe behavioral abnormalities.
D
Fruity acetone breath odor and deep Kussmaul respirations
Fruity breath and Kussmaul respirations indicate diabetic ketoacidosis rather than phenylketonuria.
E
Generalized anasarca and coarse facial features with macroglossia
Anasarca and macroglossia are unrelated to untreated autosomal recessive phenylketonuria.
q.obj: Untreated PKU causes digestive problems/vomiting, seizures, musty urine odor, intellectual disability, and in older children eczema, hypertonia, hypopigmentation, and behavioral abnormalities.
fc: All children: digestive problems/vomiting, seizures, musty urine odor, intellectual disability | Older children: eczema, hypertonia, hypopigmentation (hair/skin/irises) | Behavioral abnormalities: hyperactivity, bizarre/schizoid behavior

q.st: The nurse is evaluating parents' understanding of dietary management for their infant newly diagnosed with phenylketonuria (PKU). Which parental statements indicate accurate understanding? Select all that apply.
o: A
We must avoid high-protein foods like meats and dairy products because they contain high phenylalanine
Meats and dairy products are rich in phenylalanine and must be excluded from the PKU diet.
B
We need to read food labels closely because the artificial sweetener aspartame contains phenylalanine
Aspartame breaks down into phenylalanine and must be strictly avoided by checking all food labels.
C
Cereals, pastas, rice, fruits, and vegetables are safe foods for our child to eat
Low-protein grains, fruits, and vegetables provide safe calories alongside prescribed phenylalanine-free formulas.
D
Once our child reaches age 5, a normal high-protein diet can be resumed permanently
Lifelong dietary restriction and regular follow-up appointments are required to prevent neurocognitive damage.
E
Standard cow's milk infant formula can be mixed 50-50 with water to meet protein needs
Infants with PKU require specially prepared low-phenylalanine formulas rather than standard cow's milk formulas.
q.obj: PKU dietary management restricts phenylalanine by avoiding high-protein foods (meats, dairy) and aspartame, using special formulas, and allowing cereals, pastas, rice, fruits, and vegetables.
fc: Primary treatment: lifelong phenylalanine-restricted diet + special formulas | AVOID: high-protein foods (meats, dairy) and aspartame (artificial sweetener) | ALLOWED: cereals, pastas, rice, fruits, vegetables; consult social services for formula cost
Ch. 33 Section III.C.4 & Clinical Judgment Box

q.st: The parents of an infant diagnosed with phenylketonuria express concern about the high out-of-pocket expense of purchasing specially prepared phenylalanine-free medical formulas. Which interprofessional referral should the nurse initiate?
o: A
Consult social care services to assist with the financial burden of special formulas
Social care services help families access financial assistance programs for costly prescribed PKU formulas.
B
Refer the family to physical therapy to teach exercises that metabolize phenylalanine
Exercise cannot substitute for the missing hepatic enzyme or reduce dietary phenylalanine toxicity.
C
Advise the parents to substitute soy-based commercial formula to save money
Commercial soy formulas contain high protein and phenylalanine and cause severe neurotoxicity in PKU.
D
Consult occupational therapy to introduce high-protein solid foods earlier
High-protein solid foods are contraindicated in infants and children with phenylketonuria.
q.obj: The nurse should consult with social care services to assist parents with the financial burdens of purchasing special prepared PKU formulas.
fc: Consult social care services for financial assistance with special formulas | Monitor physical, neurological, and intellectual development | Discuss autosomal recessive inheritance risk in future pregnancies

q.st: During genetic counseling follow-up for a toddler with phenylketonuria (PKU), the parents ask about the chance of having another child with PKU in a future pregnancy. Which genetic principle guides the nurse's discussion?
o: A
PKU is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder carrying a recurrence risk in future children
Because PKU is autosomal recessive, carrier parents carry a recurrence risk in future children.
B
PKU is caused by a spontaneous maternal viral infection and will not recur
PKU is an inherited autosomal recessive metabolic disorder rather than a sporadic viral illness.
C
PKU is an X-linked dominant disorder that affects only male offspring
Autosomal recessive inheritance affects males and females equally rather than following X-linked transmission.
D
PKU is prevented in future pregnancies by taking prenatal vitamin B12 supplements
Autosomal recessive gene transmission cannot be prevented by maternal prenatal vitamin supplementation.
q.obj: Phenylketonuria is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder; nurses should discuss the risk of phenylketonuria in future children with parents.
fc: Mode of inheritance: autosomal recessive genetic disorder | Encourage parents to express feelings about diagnosis | Discuss genetic risk of PKU in future children

q.st: During a well-child visit, the nurse calculates the body mass index (BMI) percentile for a 10-year-old child and plots it at the 96th percentile for age and sex. How does the CDC classify this child's weight status?
o: A
Obesity (BMI greater than the 95th percentile)
CDC standards define childhood obesity as a BMI greater than the 95th percentile for ages 2-20.
B
Overweight (BMI between the 85th and 95th percentiles)
Overweight is defined as above the 85th percentile but less than the 95th percentile.
C
Healthy weight (BMI below the 85th percentile)
A BMI at the 96th percentile exceeds both healthy weight and overweight pediatric thresholds.
D
Severe obesity (defined strictly as BMI greater than the 50th percentile)
Severe obesity is defined as BMI >= 120% of the 95th percentile or BMI >= 35.
q.obj: For ages 2-20, CDC BMI percentiles define overweight as >85th to <95th percentile, obesity as >95th percentile, and severe obesity as >=120% of the 95th percentile or BMI >=35.
fc: BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)^2 | Overweight: > 85th percentile and < 95th percentile | Obesity: > 95th percentile; Severe obesity: >= 120% of 95th percentile or BMI >= 35

q.st: A 14-year-old adolescent has a BMI equal to 125% of the 95th percentile for age and sex. Which classification accurately describes this adolescent's status?
o: A
Severe obesity
A BMI at or above 120% of the 95th percentile defines severe pediatric obesity.
B
Overweight
Overweight applies only to children whose BMI falls between the 85th and 95th percentiles.
C
Moderate obesity
CDC pediatric criteria categorize BMI >= 120% of the 95th percentile specifically as severe obesity.
D
Normal adolescent growth spurt
A BMI at 125% of the 95th percentile represents severe obesity requiring medical and lifestyle intervention.
q.obj: Severe obesity in children and adolescents is defined as a BMI greater than or equal to 120% of the 95th percentile or a BMI >= 35.
fc: Severe obesity: BMI >= 120% of the 95th percentile OR BMI >= 35 | Requires screening for comorbidities (type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, sleep apnea) | Increases risk of adult obesity and metabolic syndrome

q.st: The nurse is counseling the parents of an 11-year-old child diagnosed with childhood obesity about associated health risks. Which comorbidities and long-term complications are linked to childhood obesity? Select all that apply.
o: A
Type 2 diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia leading to heart disease
Excess adiposity promotes insulin resistance and dyslipidemia, increasing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk.
B
Obstructive sleep apnea, asthma, and bone and joint problems
Excess body weight compromises airway patency, exacerbates asthma, and places mechanical stress on growing joints.
C
Adult obesity with metabolic syndrome, cancer, and psychosocial health problems
Obese children are likely to remain obese as adults with physical, social, and emotional complications.
D
Autosomal recessive phenylketonuria and congenital hypothyroidism
Phenylketonuria and congenital hypothyroidism are congenital genetic/endocrine disorders unrelated to childhood obesity.
E
Acute lymphocytic leukemia and nephroblastoma
Leukemia and Wilms' tumor are pediatric malignancies not caused by childhood obesity.
q.obj: Childhood obesity increases risks for asthma, sleep apnea, bone/joint problems, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, psychosocial issues, and adult obesity with heart disease, metabolic syndrome, and cancer.
fc: Childhood comorbidities: asthma, sleep apnea, bone/joint problems, type 2 DM, hyperlipidemia | Psychosocial: physical, social, and emotional health problems | Adult risk: adult obesity, type 2 DM, heart disease, metabolic syndrome, cancer

q.st: The nurse is educating a community parent group on pediatric metabolic health. What is the number one risk factor for developing type 2 diabetes mellitus in childhood?
o: A
Being overweight
Being overweight is the leading risk factor driving the rising incidence of pediatric type 2 diabetes.
B
Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
Autoimmune pancreatic beta-cell destruction causes absolute insulin deficiency in type 1 diabetes mellitus.
C
Recurrent viral upper respiratory infections in infancy
Viral infections do not represent the primary risk factor for insulin-resistant pediatric type 2 diabetes.
D
Excessive intake of low-phenylalanine medical formulas
Low-phenylalanine formulas treat phenylketonuria and are unrelated to childhood type 2 diabetes.
q.obj: Being overweight is the number one risk factor for developing type 2 diabetes mellitus in childhood.
fc: Type 1 DM: pancreatic beta-cell destruction -> absolute insulin deficiency | Type 2 DM: insulin resistance + relative insulin deficiency | #1 risk factor for childhood type 2 DM: being overweight

q.st: The school nurse is teaching parents and children strategies to prevent type 2 diabetes mellitus in childhood. Which lifestyle recommendations should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: A
Accumulate 60 minutes of daily physical activity such as biking, dancing, or brisk walking
At least 60 minutes of daily moderate-to-vigorous physical activity improves insulin sensitivity and weight.
B
Limit recreational screen time on computers, tablets, and phones to 60 minutes per day
Restricting sedentary screen time to 60 minutes daily reduces inactivity and supports healthy weight.
C
Drink water instead of sugared beverages and choose fresh or water-packed fruits and vegetables
Eliminating sugary sodas/juices and fast food while eating produce prevents excess caloric weight gain.
D
Replace afternoon snacks with fruit-flavored sports drinks and canned fruit in heavy syrup
Sports drinks and syrup-packed fruits contain high concentrated sugars that promote obesity.
E
Encourage 3 hours of daily television viewing after school to conserve metabolic energy
Prolonged sedentary screen time increases obesity risk and contradicts type 2 diabetes prevention guidelines.
q.obj: Preventing childhood type 2 diabetes involves drinking water instead of sugary drinks, eating fresh/water-packed produce, limiting fast food, 60 min daily exercise, and <=60 min screen time.
fc: Diet: drink water (no sodas/juices/sports drinks); fresh/frozen/water-canned produce; limit fast food | Activity: 60 min/day physical activity; limit screen time to 60 min/day | Warning signs: increased thirst, nighttime urination, blurry vision, fatigue

q.st: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric clinic for unexplained weight loss, fatigue, and frequent urination. Which additional assessment findings support a new diagnosis of diabetes mellitus? Select all that apply.
o: A
Polydipsia, polyphagia, and blurred vision
Hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis (polyuria), compensatory thirst (polydipsia), cellular hunger (polyphagia), and lens swelling.
B
Occasional nocturnal enuresis in a previously toilet-trained child
Osmotic polyuria from glycosuria frequently causes new bedwetting in a previously toilet-trained child.
C
Recurrent Candida vaginitis and slow wound healing
Hyperglycemic tissues promote Candida yeast growth and impair microvascular wound healing.
D
Weight gain with bradycardia and cold intolerance
Weight gain and cold intolerance characterize hypothyroidism rather than insulin-deficient diabetes mellitus.
E
Hypoglycemia with blood glucose consistently below 50 mg/dL
Untreated diabetes mellitus presents with elevated blood glucose (normal fasting 70-99 mg/dL) rather than hypoglycemia.
q.obj: Diabetes mellitus cues include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, hyperglycemia (normal 70-99 mg/dL), weight loss, fatigue, enuresis, adolescent Candida vaginitis, fruity breath, and slow healing.
fc: Classic triad: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia + hyperglycemia (normal 70-99 mg/dL) | Pediatric cues: weight loss, fatigue, enuresis in toilet-trained child, Candida vaginitis | Advanced: fruity breath, dehydration, blurred vision, slow healing, LOC changes

q.st: The nurse is explaining to the parents of a child newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus how insulin deficiency leads to diabetic ketoacidosis (Fig. 33.1). Which sequence accurately describes this pathophysiological cascade?
o: A
Insulin deficiency impairs nutrient metabolism, causing hyperglycemia, polyuria, cellular starvation, and ketone buildup
Without insulin, cells starve despite hyperglycemia and break down fats into acidic ketones.
B
Excessive insulin secretion forces glucose into cells, causing severe hypoglycemia and lactic alkalosis
Type 1 diabetes results from absolute insulin deficiency rather than excessive insulin secretion.
C
Insulin deficiency blocks renal ketone excretion, causing water intoxication and hyponatremic edema
Hyperglycemia causes osmotic polyuria and severe dehydration rather than water intoxication.
D
Cellular starvation stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release glucagon that neutralizes blood acids
Ketones accumulate because cells cannot use them without insulin, producing metabolic ketoacidosis.
q.obj: Insulin deficiency impairs fat/protein/carbohydrate metabolism -> hyperglycemia -> polyuria and cellular starvation -> ketone production that cannot nourish cells -> ketoacidosis.
fc: Insulin deficiency -> impaired metabolism of fats, proteins, carbohydrates | Hyperglycemia (fatigue, hunger, weight loss) -> polyuria & cellular starvation | Ketones produced for starvation cannot nourish cells without insulin -> ketoacidosis

q.st: A 9-year-old child is newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus during an inpatient admission. Which interprofessional consultation is a priority for planning the child's comprehensive care?
o: A
Initiate a consultation with a diabetic specialist to plan the child's care
For a child with diabetes mellitus, the nurse plans to initiate a diabetic specialist consultation.
B
Refer the child exclusively to a pediatric surgeon for pancreatic transplantation
Medical management with exogenous insulin, nutrition, and diabetes specialist care is the standard approach.
C
Consult a speech-language pathologist to evaluate dysphagia prior to oral fluids
Routine diabetes care requires a diabetic specialist rather than speech-language pathology.
D
Schedule genetic counseling for autosomal recessive carrier testing of siblings
Diabetes specialist consultation is the priority safety action for planning pediatric diabetes management.
q.obj: For a child with diabetes mellitus, the nurse should plan to initiate a consultation with the diabetic specialist to plan the child's care.
fc: Initiate consultation with the diabetic specialist to plan the child's care | Long-term effects to prevent: growth failure, delayed maturation, infections, neuropathy, CV/retinal/renal microvascular disease

q.st: The nurse is teaching the parents of an 8-year-old child with type 1 diabetes mellitus how to structure the child's daily meal plan. Which dietary principles are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: A
Provide three well-balanced meals at regular intervals plus midafternoon and bedtime snacks
Consistent meal timing with midafternoon and bedtime snacks balances insulin peaks and prevents hypoglycemia.
B
Maintain consistent prescribed protein, fat (<=30% of calories), and carbohydrates while avoiding concentrated sweets
Consistent macronutrient distribution and limiting concentrated sweets stabilize blood glucose without special diet foods.
C
Incorporate cultural preferences, allow the child to make food choices, and carry glucose tablets at all times
Child participation builds autonomy, cultural adaptation supports adherence, and glucose tablets treat sudden hypoglycemia.
D
Purchase specialized sugar-free diabetic supplements to replace normal family meals
Children with diabetes need normal healthy nutrition rather than special diabetic foods or supplements.
E
Eliminate all dietary carbohydrates so exogenous insulin doses can be discontinued
Growing children require individualized carbohydrates and exogenous insulin for normal growth and development.
q.obj: Pediatric diabetes nutrition includes normal healthy food (no special supplements), 3 regular meals + midafternoon/bedtime snacks, consistent macronutrients (fat <=30%), child food choices, and carrying glucose.
fc: No special diabetic foods; 3 regular balanced meals + midafternoon & bedtime snacks | Consistent protein, fat (<= 30% calories), and carbs; avoid concentrated sweets | Include child in food choices; carry glucose source (tablets) at all times

q.st: A school-age child with type 1 diabetes mellitus plans to participate in a 45-minute after-school soccer practice. Which instruction should the school nurse provide to prevent exercise-induced hypoglycemia?
o: A
Check blood glucose before and after practice and eat 10 to 15 g of carbohydrates (e.g., small box of raisins or juice)
Exercise increases glucose use, requiring 10 to 15 g of extra carbohydrates per session.
B
Administer half the prescribed morning insulin dose on days when soccer practice is scheduled
Insulin doses should not be arbitrarily reduced without a primary health care provider prescription.
C
Eat twice the normal amount of food at lunch and skip the bedtime snack
Doubling lunch causes postprandial hyperglycemia, and skipping the bedtime snack risks nocturnal hypoglycemia.
D
Delay morning insulin administration until immediately before afternoon soccer practice
Altering prescribed insulin timing disrupts daytime glycemic control and risks ketoacidosis.
q.obj: For exercise, children with diabetes should monitor blood glucose before and after activity and consume extra carbohydrates—usually 10 to 15 g for every 30 to 45 minutes of activity.
fc: Consume extra food: 10 to 15 g carbohydrates for every 30 to 45 minutes of activity | Examples: small box of raisins or cup of orange juice | Check blood glucose before and after exercising; do not alter insulin unprescribed

q.st: The nurse is reviewing long-term complications of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus with an adolescent client. Which chronic microvascular and developmental complications can occur?
o: A
Failure to grow at a normal rate, delayed maturation, retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy
Chronic hyperglycemia impairs childhood growth/maturation and damages retinal, renal, cardiovascular, and peripheral nerve tissues.
B
Precocious puberty, gigantism, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Poorly controlled diabetes causes growth failure and delayed maturation rather than gigantism or precocious puberty.
C
Autosomal recessive enzyme deficiency and cranial suture craniosynostosis
Enzyme deficiencies and craniosynostosis are congenital conditions rather than chronic diabetic complications.
D
Hyperparathyroidism and osteogenic sarcoma of the distal femur
Hyperparathyroidism and bone sarcomas are unrelated to chronic microvascular complications of diabetes.
q.obj: Long-term effects of pediatric diabetes include growth failure, delayed maturation, recurrent infections, neuropathy, cardiovascular disease, and retinal and renal microvascular disease.
fc: Long-Term Effects & Complications of Pediatric DM

Growth/Development: failure to grow at normal rate, delayed maturation, recurrent infections | Microvascular/Macrovascular: neuropathy, retinopathy, nephropathy, cardiovascular disease | Acute complications: hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, DKA, coma, K+ imbalances

q.st: The nurse is teaching the parents of an infant newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus about safe insulin therapy and laboratory monitoring. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: A
Label diluted insulin clearly to avoid dosage errors and always keep a spare bottle available
Infants may need diluted insulin; clear labeling and spare vials prevent dosing errors.
B
Schedule glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) testing every 3 months, aiming for a reference value <6%
HbA1c reflects 3-month glycemic control and should be evaluated quarterly with a target below 6%.
C
Obtain a MedicAlert bracelet listing the child's prescribed insulin type and daily dosage
Medical identification alerts emergency responders to the child's insulin dependence and dosing regimen.
D
Withhold all insulin whenever the infant develops an acute viral illness or infection
Illness and infection increase insulin requirements; withholding insulin precipitates life-threatening diabetic ketoacidosis.
E
Administer the morning insulin dose as usual before surgery when the infant is NPO
When a child is NPO for a procedure, verify morning insulin with the provider.
q.obj: Insulin safety includes clearly labeled diluted insulin for infants, spare vials, MedicAlert bracelet, HbA1c <6% every 3 months, never withholding insulin during illness, and verifying NPO doses.
fc: Diluted insulin for infants: label clearly; always keep spare bottle; wear MedicAlert bracelet | HbA1c: check every 3 months (reference interval < 6%) | NEVER withhold insulin during illness/infection/stress; verify NPO doses with PHCP

q.st: A 10-year-old child with type 1 diabetes mellitus is scheduled for an outpatient tonsillectomy and will be NPO (nothing by mouth) starting at midnight. Which action should the nurse take regarding the morning insulin dose?
o: A
Verify with the primary health care provider whether to withhold morning insulin and when to resume it
When a child is NPO for a procedure, morning insulin must be verified with the PHCP.
B
Administer the full usual morning dose of rapid-acting and long-acting insulin at 6 AM
Administering full rapid-acting insulin to a fasting NPO child causes severe preoperative hypoglycemia.
C
Instruct the parents to permanently discontinue insulin for 48 hours before any surgery
Completely omitting basal insulin in type 1 diabetes precipitates dangerous surgical diabetic ketoacidosis.
D
Give 8 ounces of orange juice with the morning insulin 1 hour before anesthesia
Oral liquids violate NPO anesthesia safety guidelines and risk intraoperative pulmonary aspiration.
q.obj: When a child with diabetes is NPO for a special procedure, the nurse must verify with the PHCP the need to withhold morning insulin and when food, fluids, and insulin resume.
fc: When child is NPO for a special procedure: verify with PHCP need to withhold morning insulin | Also clarify when food, fluids, and insulin are to be resumed | Contrast with sick days: never withhold insulin during illness without PHCP order

q.st: The nurse is teaching a 9-year-old child with type 1 diabetes mellitus how to lessen the pain of fingerstick blood glucose monitoring. Which technique should the nurse demonstrate?
o: A
Warm the finger under water and puncture just to the side of the ring finger pad
Warming enhances blood flow and the side of the ring finger has fewer nerve endings.
B
Puncture directly in the center of the index finger pad using maximum lancet depth
The center of the index finger pad is densely innervated and causes maximal puncture pain.
C
Clean the finger with rubbing alcohol and puncture while the skin is still wet
Puncturing wet alcohol stings intensely and can hemolyze or dilute the capillary blood sample.
D
Press the lancet device firmly into the skin to obtain a large drop of blood
Pressing lightly prevents deep painful punctures while micro-sample meters require only tiny blood drops.
q.obj: To lessen blood glucose monitoring pain, warm the finger under water, puncture the side of the ring finger or thumb pad, press the lancet lightly, and use micro-sample meters.
fc: Lessening Pain of Blood Glucose Monitoring (Box 33.2)

Hold finger under warm water for a few seconds before puncture | Use ring finger or thumb; puncture just to the SIDE of the finger pad | Press lancet lightly against skin; use monitors requiring small blood samples

q.st: An adolescent with type 1 diabetes mellitus obtains a fingerstick blood glucose reading of 412 mg/dL, which seems unusually high given the child's current asymptomatic status. Which action should the nurse instruct the adolescent to take first?
o: A
Reread instructions, reassess technique, check test strip expiration dates, and repeat the test
Unreasonable glucose readings require verifying technique, meter calibration, and strip expiration dates before repeating.
B
Immediately inject a double dose of regular insulin to bring the reading down quickly
Administering extra insulin based on a potentially erroneous reading risks life-threatening hypoglycemic coma.
C
Ignore the high reading and retest at the same time the following morning
Ignoring a markedly elevated reading could miss impending diabetic ketoacidosis if the result is accurate.
D
Test a first-voided urine specimen for glucose instead of repeating the blood test
Blood glucose monitoring is far more accurate than unreliable urine glucose testing.
q.obj: If blood glucose results do not seem reasonable, instruct the child and parents to reread instructions, reassess technique, check test strip expiration dates, and repeat the test.
fc: Blood glucose monitoring is more accurate than urine glucose testing | Wash hands before/after; calibrate monitor per manufacturer; check strip expiration date | Unreasonable result: reread instructions, check technique/strips, and repeat test

q.st: The nurse is educating the parents of a child with type 1 diabetes mellitus about the role of urine testing in diabetes management. Which statement accurately reflects nursing guidelines for urine testing?
o: A
Urine glucose testing is unreliable, but urine must be tested for ketones when ill or glucose exceeds 200 mg/dL
Urine ketone testing on a second-voided specimen detects impending ketoacidosis during illness or hyperglycemia >200 mg/dL.
B
First-voided morning urine glucose testing is the gold standard for adjusting daily insulin doses
Blood glucose monitoring is much more accurate than urine glucose testing, and second-voided specimens are best.
C
Urine ketone testing is only necessary when blood glucose drops below 70 mg/dL
Ketones develop during insulin deficiency and hyperglycemia (>200 mg/dL) or illness rather than hypoglycemia.
D
Trace urinary ketones are a normal expected finding after every high-protein meal
The presence of urinary ketones indicates fat breakdown and impending diabetic ketoacidosis.
q.obj: Urine glucose testing is unreliable, but urine must be tested for ketones (using a second-voided specimen) when the child is ill or blood glucose is consistently >200 mg/dL.
fc: Urine glucose testing is unreliable; second-voided urine specimen is most accurate | Test urine for KETONES when child is ill OR blood glucose consistently > 200 mg/dL | Presence of urinary ketones indicates impending ketoacidosis

q.st: The parents of a 7-year-old child with type 1 diabetes mellitus ask how to prepare for a severe hypoglycemic episode in which the child becomes semiconscious and cannot swallow safely. Which emergency medication should the nurse teach the parents to administer?
o: A
Intramuscular or subcutaneous glucagon
Glucagon is given IM or SC when a hypoglycemic child is unconscious or semiconscious.
B
Subcutaneous regular insulin
Administering insulin during hypoglycemia fatally worsens neuroglycopenia and brain injury.
C
Oral orange juice poured slowly into the back of the throat
Pouring liquids into the mouth of a semiconscious child poses a severe pulmonary aspiration hazard.
D
Rectal sodium polystyrene sulfonate suspension
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate lowers potassium and has no effect on blood glucose levels.
q.obj: Parents must be instructed in administering glucagon intramuscularly or subcutaneously if the child has a hypoglycemic reaction and is unable to consume anything orally (semiconscious/unconscious).
fc: Indication: hypoglycemic child is semiconscious/unconscious and cannot take oral glucose | Route: intramuscular (IM) or subcutaneous (SC) by trained parents | Hospital alternative: IV dextrose if unable to take oral glucose

q.st: A 10-year-old child with type 1 diabetes mellitus returns from gym class reporting dizziness and hunger. Which clinical manifestations indicate hypoglycemia (blood glucose less than 70 mg/dL)? Select all that apply.
o: A
Sweating, tremors, pallor, and anxiety
Adrenergic sympathetic activation during hypoglycemia produces diaphoresis, shakiness, and acute anxiety.
B
Headache, nausea, lethargy, confusion, and slurred speech
Cerebral glucose deprivation (neuroglycopenia) causes headache, lethargy, confusion, and slurred speech.
C
Tingling sensation around the mouth and intense hunger
Perioral paresthesias and sudden hunger are classic early autonomic cues of blood glucose <70 mg/dL.
D
Fruity acetone breath odor and deep Kussmaul respirations
Fruity breath and Kussmaul respirations are hallmark signs of hyperglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis.
E
Flushed, dry skin with extreme polyuria and polydipsia
Flushed dry skin and polyuria characterize hyperglycemia rather than acute hypoglycemia.
q.obj: Hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL [4 mmol/L]) results from excess insulin, inadequate food, or excessive activity, causing headache, nausea, sweating, tremors, lethargy, hunger, confusion, slurred speech, and perioral tingling.
fc: Definition: blood glucose < 70 mg/dL (4 mmol/L); Causes: too much insulin, too little food, excess activity | Autonomic cues: sweating, tremors, hunger, anxiety, tingling around mouth | Neuroglycopenic cues: headache, nausea, lethargy, confusion, slurred speech

q.st: A conscious 8-year-old child with type 1 diabetes mellitus has a blood glucose reading of 58 mg/dL (3.2 mmol/L). Which rapid-acting food items from Box 33.3 are appropriate to treat this episode? Select all that apply.
o: A
1/2 cup of orange juice or 2 to 3 glucose tablets
Half a cup of orange juice or 2-3 glucose tablets provides fast-absorbing simple carbohydrate.
B
1 teaspoon of honey or 1 small box of raisins
A teaspoon of honey or small box of raisins rapidly elevates blood glucose in conscious children.
C
8 oz of milk or 3 to 4 hard candies (such as Life Savers)
Eight ounces of milk, 3-4 hard candies, or 4 sugar cubes are approved rapid glucose sources.
D
1 cup of sugar-free diet soda
Diet carbonated beverages contain artificial sweeteners with zero glucose and will not treat hypoglycemia.
E
2 slices of plain grilled turkey breast
Protein alone without simple carbohydrate does not rapidly raise falling blood glucose levels.
q.obj: Approved rapid-acting hypoglycemia items include 1/2 cup orange juice/regular soda, 8 oz milk, small box of raisins, 3-4 hard candies/Life Savers, 4 sugar cubes, 1 candy bar, 1 tsp honey, or 2-3 glucose tablets.
fc: 1/2 cup orange juice or regular soda; 8 oz milk; 1 small box raisins | 3-4 hard candies or Life Savers; 4 sugar cubes (1 Tbsp sugar); 1 candy bar | 1 tsp honey; 2-3 glucose tablets

q.st: The nurse is caring for a child older than 2 years with type 1 diabetes mellitus who has a blood glucose level of 60 mg/dL (3.4 mmol/L). Which nursing interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
o: A
Give 1 teaspoon of honey immediately, followed by a complex carbohydrate and protein snack
Rapid-releasing glucose must be followed by complex carbohydrate and protein to sustain blood glucose.
B
Prepare to administer subcutaneous glucagon if unconsciousness occurs
If the child becomes unconscious and cannot swallow, glucagon or IV dextrose is required.
C
Check vital signs, retest blood glucose, and give an extra snack if the next meal is >30 minutes away
Retesting blood glucose and providing a snack when meals are >30 minutes away prevents rebound hypoglycemia.
D
Administer a small dose of regular insulin to stabilize glucose transport
Insulin lowers blood glucose further and is strictly contraindicated during acute hypoglycemia.
E
Encourage brisk hallway ambulation for 15 minutes before retesting blood glucose
Physical activity consumes circulating glucose and worsens acute hypoglycemia in diabetic pediatric clients.
q.obj: Hypoglycemia care: give rapid glucose + complex carb/protein, check VS, retest glucose, give snack if meal >30 min away; if unconscious, apply glucose paste to gums and retest in 15 min, or give glucagon/IV dextrose.
fc: Conscious: rapid glucose -> follow with complex carb + protein (bread/peanut butter cracker) | Retest glucose; give extra snack if next meal > 30 min away or activity planned | Unconscious: cake frosting/glucose paste on gums, retest in 15 min; glucagon or IV dextrose

q.st: A 7-year-old child with type 1 diabetes mellitus becomes unconscious at home during a severe hypoglycemic reaction. After squeezing glucose paste onto the child's gums, when should the parent retest the blood glucose level?
o: A
In 15 minutes, administering additional glucose or glucagon if the reading remains low
Apply glucose paste to gums and retest in 15 minutes; give glucagon if low.
B
In 60 minutes after allowing the child to sleep undisturbed
Waiting 60 minutes during unconscious hypoglycemia risks permanent hypoglycemic brain damage.
C
Immediately after pouring 8 ounces of apple juice into the child's mouth
Oral liquids must never be poured into an unconscious child's mouth due to aspiration.
D
In 2 hours after administering the child's scheduled evening insulin dose
Scheduled evening insulin must never be administered during an acute unconscious hypoglycemic episode.
q.obj: If a hypoglycemic child becomes unconscious, squeeze cake frosting or glucose paste onto the gums and retest blood glucose in 15 minutes; if still low or unconscious, give glucagon.
fc: Squeeze cake frosting or glucose paste onto gums (never pour liquids) | Retest blood glucose level in 15 minutes and monitor closely | If reading remains low or child stays unconscious -> administer glucagon (or IV dextrose in hospital)

q.st: The clinic nurse is reviewing sick day rules with the parents of a 6-year-old child who has type 1 diabetes mellitus and a mild viral upper respiratory infection. Which instructions should the nurse provide? Select all that apply.
o: A
Always give insulin even if the child lacks an appetite, and encourage liquids to clear ketones
Illness raises stress hormones and insulin needs, while fluids help flush accumulated urinary ketones.
B
Test blood glucose at least every 4 hours and test for urinary ketones with each voiding
Frequent glucose and every-void ketone monitoring detects impending diabetic ketoacidosis early.
C
Notify the PHCP if moderate/large ketones, vomiting, fruity breath, or deep rapid respirations occur
Moderate/large ketonuria, vomiting, Kussmaul respirations, or decreased consciousness indicate impending DKA.
D
Hold all insulin doses until the child resumes eating three full solid meals
Withholding insulin during illness precipitates severe hyperglycemia and life-threatening diabetic ketoacidosis.
E
Encourage vigorous outdoor exercise during illness to burn off excess blood glucose
Rest is recommended during illness, especially if urinary ketones are present.
q.obj: Sick day rules: always give insulin, test glucose at least every 4 hours, test urine ketones with every void, encourage fluids and rest, and call PHCP for ketones, vomiting, fruity breath, or Kussmaul respirations.
fc: Sick Day Rules for a Diabetic Child (Boxes 33.5-33.6 & PQ 2)

ALWAYS give insulin even if poor appetite; follow usual meal plan; encourage liquids & rest | Test blood glucose >= q4h; test urine ketones with EACH voiding | Call PHCP: blood glucose > 200, moderate/high ketones, vomiting > 1x, fruity breath, deep rapid respirations

q.st: The parents of a 6-year-old child with type 1 diabetes mellitus call the clinic reporting that the child has a mild cold, a blood glucose of 235 mg/dL, and small urinary ketones, but is alert and tolerating fluids. Which instruction should the nurse give?
o: A
Encourage the child to drink liquids to aid in clearing ketones and continue insulin as prescribed
Liquids are essential to clear urinary ketones, and prescribed insulin must be continued during illness.
B
Hold the next scheduled dose of insulin until the urinary ketones clear completely
Holding insulin during ketonuria worsens insulin deficiency and accelerates progression to diabetic ketoacidosis.
C
Administer a double dose of regular insulin at home without provider orders
Parents should never arbitrarily double insulin doses without specific primary health care provider instructions.
D
Restrict oral fluids for 4 hours so the next urine specimen is more concentrated
Restricting fluids worsens dehydration and impairs renal clearance of ketone bodies.
q.obj: During illness with ketonuria, liquids are essential to aid in clearing ketones, insulin must be continued, and blood glucose/ketones must be monitored closely.
fc: Managing Ketonuria on Sick Days (Box 33.6 & PQ 2)
Encourage liquids to aid in clearing urinary ketones | Continue prescribed insulin; encourage rest when ketones are present | Notify PHCP if moderate/large ketones, vomiting, or DKA signs develop

q.st: An adolescent with type 1 diabetes mellitus is admitted to the emergency department with suspected diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Which laboratory and physical assessment findings are characteristic of DKA?
o: A
Blood glucose >300 mg/dL, positive ketones, Kussmaul's respirations, fruity breath, and decreasing LOC
DKA features blood glucose >300 mg/dL, positive serum/urine ketones, Kussmaul's respirations, acetone breath, and lethargy.
B
Blood glucose <60 mg/dL, negative ketones, sweating, tremors, and hypertension
Low blood glucose with sweating and tremors indicates acute hypoglycemia rather than diabetic ketoacidosis.
C
Blood glucose of 140 mg/dL, bradypnea, peripheral edema, and bounding pulses
DKA presents with severe dehydration (hypotension) and deep rapid Kussmaul's respirations rather than edema.
D
Normal blood glucose of 90 mg/dL, hyperactive reflexes, and positive Trousseau's sign
Normal glucose and hypocalcemic tetany are inconsistent with severe insulin-deficient diabetic ketoacidosis.
q.obj: Diabetic ketoacidosis (blood glucose >300 mg/dL [17.14 mmol/L], positive urine/serum ketones) presents with hyperglycemia signs, Kussmaul's respirations, acetone (fruity) breath, lethargy, and decreasing LOC.
fc: Blood glucose > 300 mg/dL (17.14 mmol/L) + positive urine & serum ketones | Kussmaul's respirations (deep, rapid) + acetone (fruity) breath odor | Dehydration, increasing lethargy, and decreasing level of consciousness
Ch. 33 Section V.L.1, Safety Alert & PQ 4

q.st: A 10-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with abdominal pain, lethargy, Kussmaul's respirations, and a blood glucose of 485 mg/dL, confirming diabetic ketoacidosis. Which intravenous infusion should the nurse prepare to administer first?
o: A
Normal saline (0.9% sodium chloride) infusion
Restoring circulating blood volume with normal saline is the initial priority step in resolving DKA.
B
5% dextrose in water (D5W) infusion
Dextrose solutions are added only later once blood glucose decreases to an appropriate target level.
C
Intravenous NPH intermediate-acting insulin infusion
Only regular insulin is administered intravenously; NPH insulin is never given by the IV route.
D
Intravenous potassium chloride bolus prior to fluid resuscitation
Potassium is added only after initial hydration confirms adequate urinary output and potassium levels.
q.obj: Initial treatment of DKA focuses on restoring circulating blood volume with IV infusions of 0.9% or 0.45% saline before IV regular insulin and later dextrose addition.
fc: Step 1: Restore circulating volume with IV 0.9% (normal) or 0.45% saline | Step 2: Correct hyperglycemia with IV REGULAR insulin (never NPH IV) | Step 3: Add IV dextrose when blood glucose reaches an appropriate level

q.st: A child with diabetic ketoacidosis is receiving continuous intravenous regular insulin and normal saline. Why must the nurse monitor serum potassium levels closely during intravenous insulin therapy?
o: A
Intravenous insulin shifts potassium out of the bloodstream into cells, causing serum potassium to drop
As insulin lowers blood glucose, potassium moves intracellularly, potentially causing life-threatening hypokalemia.
B
Regular insulin stimulates renal tubular potassium retention, causing rapid hyperkalemia
Insulin drives potassium into cells and lowers serum levels rather than causing renal potassium retention.
C
Normal saline chelates serum potassium into an inactive complex excreted in stool
Normal saline restores vascular volume; intracellular potassium shifting is driven by intravenous regular insulin.
D
Ketone clearance releases large amounts of potassium from adipose tissue into plasma
Correcting acidosis and giving insulin shifts potassium into cells, requiring replacement once voiding is confirmed.
q.obj: During DKA treatment, monitor serum potassium closely because IV insulin shifts potassium into cells and lowers serum potassium, often requiring replacement once adequate voiding is confirmed.
fc: Monitor serum potassium closely during IV regular insulin infusion | Insulin lowers blood glucose AND drives potassium into cells (risks hypokalemia) | Ensure child is VOIDNG adequately before administering IV potassium (prevents hyperkalemia)

q.st: A child being treated for diabetic ketoacidosis with intravenous normal saline and regular insulin now has a blood glucose level that has decreased from 510 mg/dL to 220 mg/dL. Which prescription change should the nurse anticipate?
o: A
Addition of intravenous dextrose to the infusion fluid while continuing insulin to clear ketones
IV dextrose is added when blood glucose reaches an appropriate level to prevent hypoglycemia.
B
Immediate discontinuation of all intravenous fluids and insulin therapy
Stopping insulin prematurely before ketones and acidosis resolve causes rebound diabetic ketoacidosis.
C
Administration of subcutaneous glucagon to raise blood glucose back above 400 mg/dL
Glucagon treats severe hypoglycemia and would dangerously worsen hyperglycemia and ketosis.
D
Switching from intravenous regular insulin to intravenous glargine insulin
Regular insulin is the only insulin administered intravenously; dextrose is added to prevent hypoglycemia.
q.obj: In diabetic ketoacidosis management, IV dextrose is added as prescribed when the blood glucose reaches an appropriate level to prevent hypoglycemia while continuing ketone clearance.
fc: Continue IV regular insulin until acidosis and ketosis resolve | Add IV dextrose as prescribed when blood glucose reaches an appropriate level | Prevents iatrogenic hypoglycemia and cerebral edema during DKA correction

q.st: The nurse is caring for a 12-year-old child admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with severe diabetic ketoacidosis. Which nursing interventions are essential during acute management? Select all that apply.
o: A
Monitor vital signs, urine output, mental status, and blood glucose levels frequently
Close surveillance tracks volume resuscitation, detects cerebral edema, and guides insulin titration.
B
Administer oxygen as prescribed and monitor closely for signs of fluid overload
Supplemental oxygen supports tissue oxygenation while fluid overload monitoring prevents pulmonary or cerebral edema.
C
Identify and treat the underlying precipitating cause of hyperglycemia (such as infection)
Eliminating triggers such as occult infection prevents recurrent metabolic decompensation.
D
Administer intravenous potassium immediately before obtaining initial urine output
Potassium must never be administered intravenously until adequate urine output and renal function are verified.
E
Administer intravenous NPH insulin bolus every 2 hours until urine ketones clear
NPH insulin is never administered intravenously; only regular insulin is given IV.
q.obj: DKA management includes restoring volume (0.9%/0.45% saline), IV regular insulin, oxygen, frequent VS/urine/mental status/glucose/K+ checks, confirming voiding before K+, fluid overload checks, adding dextrose, and treating causes.
fc: IV 0.9% or 0.45% saline + IV regular insulin + prescribed oxygen | Monitor VS, urine output, mental status, blood glucose, K+ (void before K+), fluid overload | Add IV dextrose when glucose drops; treat underlying cause of hyperglycemia

q.st: A 9-year-old child receiving aggressive intravenous fluid and insulin therapy for severe diabetic ketoacidosis suddenly develops a severe headache, bradycardia, and decreasing level of consciousness despite improving blood glucose levels. Which complication should the nurse suspect first?
o: A
Cerebral edema with increased intracranial pressure requiring immediate provider notification
Sudden headache, bradycardia, and declining consciousness during DKA rehydration indicate life-threatening cerebral edema/ICP.
B
Expected drowsiness resulting from normal ketone clearance and metabolic recovery
Decreasing level of consciousness with bradycardia is a critical neurological emergency rather than normal recovery.
C
Acute hyperglycemic rebound requiring a rapid bolus of intravenous normal saline
Rapid fluid boluses worsen cerebral edema; mental status deterioration requires immediate PHCP intervention.
D
Mild symptomatic hypoglycemia that should be treated with 8 ounces of oral milk
Oral fluids are unsafe with decreasing consciousness, and bradycardia with headache points to cerebral edema.
q.obj: During DKA treatment, the nurse must monitor mental status, vital signs, and fluid overload closely to detect cerebral hypoperfusion or cerebral edema/increased ICP early.
fc: Mental Status & Fluid Overload Surveillance in DKA

Monitor mental status, vital signs, and fluid overload closely during DKA therapy | Headache, bradycardia, and decreasing LOC = acute cerebral edema / increased ICP | Protect against cerebral, coronary, and renal hypoperfusion
Ch. 33 Section V.L.2.a, d, j & Box 32.1
